en: Prosperity! Victorious is Śrī Hari!
Salutations to the venerable Rāmānuja!

In the *Siddhitraya* (The Three Treatises on Proof) graciously bestowed by the supreme teacher, the venerable Yāmunamuni—this is the *Saṃvitsiddhi* (Proof of Consciousness), accompanied by the commentary titled *Siddhāñjana*.
The scriptural word of the Upaniṣads declares: "That Brahman is indeed one, without a second."
Does it not indeed negate the existence of a Brahmā other than that [Brahmā]? // 1 //

(Commentary: May that glorious Lord—who eternally rules over the universe, for whom there exists no other object worthy of comparison, and whose knowledge is attained through the two types of Upaniṣads, the higher and the lower; who dwells within the hearts of all beings and expands their intellects according to their respective capacities—graciously bestow upon me, out of compassion, a complete blossoming of wisdom. // 1 //
Having meditated upon that yogi Lakṣmaṇa, who understood the intention of Yamunācārya,
I shall now expound the *Saṃvitsiddhi*, the work of the noble Yamuna.

Here, in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*, the nature and other characteristics of consciousness— which is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and which establishes the reality of the objects of cognition (*prameya*)— are being clarified. This is the first [work] among the three Siddhis, composed in the form of a garland of verses (*ślokamālikā*),
similar to the *Tantravārtika* and the *Ātmasiddhi* and *Iśvarasiddhi*.
Moreover, in this work, a large portion of the text is lost at the beginning, middle, and end;
and in the extant portions of the *Saṃvitsiddhi*, the refutation of the Advaita position is frequently observed.
For the Advaitins [hold that] "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," regarding that which is denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*) as the causal substrate.
Because of the scriptural hearing that the Supreme Brahman is non-dual, and because of the scriptural hearing that "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"— therefore, Brahman alone,
which is pure consciousness (cinmātra) and devoid of any commonality of difference whether of the same class, of a different class, or inherent within itself, is the existent ultimate reality;
they declare that everything else is merely superimposed upon that very [Brahman] through ignorance (avidyā) and is thus illusory.

Therein, in order to describe the impossibility of the scriptural statement regarding non-duality conveying the meaning intended by that [opponent], he first restates their position with the words "one alone" (*ekam eva*).
Because of the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the word *tat* is supplied from the latter half of the verse to the former half.
Thus, the Vedic statement of the Upanishads is: "One alone... [and so forth].

The word "tat" (that) functions as a correlative [to the relative pronoun "yat"]. Alternatively, in the second half-verse, the word "tat" refers to what is already well-known (*prasiddha*), rather than serving as a restatement (*pratinirdeśa*) of that which was indicated by the word "yat".
In the phrase "tad brahma," it is possible that the reading is "sad brahma."

The intention of the opponents (pūrvapakṣins) is that the word "non-dual" (*advitīya*), which qualifies the excellent words expressing Brahman, is intended to convey the non-existence of anything other than Brahman. // 1 //
To this we reply: regarding the expression "non-dual" (advitīya), what compound is intended?
Is it a tatpuruṣa or a bahuvrīhi? Let it be stated. (2)

In order to refute this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) analyzes the function of the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) in the following manner: "here," that is, in the expression "without a second"—or rather, the syntactical connection is: "is it a *bahuvrīhi* compound? // 2 //
In the former [type of comparison], the subsequent object is primarily intended to be the referent; in that case, "that Brahman" is either something other than it or something similar to it. (3)
Alternatively, it may be contradictory to that; yet among these three [possibilities], nothing else subverts [the argument].
Whether there is difference or similarity, the second [alternative] is certainly established. //4//
He states, with the four verses beginning with "In the former," that there is no sublation of the second [term] when the compound *advitīya* functions as a *tatpuruṣa*.
Regarding the term *tatpuruṣa*, in the first alternative, the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is intended to be predominant;
the sense is that, because a *tatpuruṣa* is one in which the meaning of the final member is predominant.
Regarding the term *tatra*: "not having a second" (*advitīya*) means "without a second.

Grammarians maintain that in a negative determinative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*), the state of being superimposed constitutes the meaning of the first member, and that this [meaning] functions as a qualifier for the meaning of the subsequent member.
And superimposition occurs upon that which is similar and so forth;

the statement of its result is that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of "other than that" (*tadanya*) and so on. This is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) of the grammarians: "When joined with *nañ* or *iva*, [a word] refers to something other than or similar to it, for such is the comprehension of the meaning."

And thus, when there is the cognition that Brahman possesses a superimposed second through the word "without a second" (*advitīya*), it results in the apprehension of either its being different from a second, its similarity to a second, or its opposition to a second.
In all three of these meanings, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of the referent of the word "second" as something distinct from Brahman;

for the point is that in the communication of a difference or a similarity having a second as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the establishment of the second as that counter-correlative is unimpeded. // 3 // 4 //
If there is contradiction, then either the second [proposition] contradicts the third, or the first contradicts the second;
for it is because that [second] is contradicted by the second that Brahman is reached. // 5 //
[Objection: "But even so, once Brahman's opposition to a second is understood, why is there not a sublation of the second? To this he replies: "Because of being opposed.
The intention here is as follows: "being a second" means having the nature of being a completer of the number two;
and "opposition to a second" [means] possessing a property that is opposed to being a second.
And that property is necessarily either "firstness" or "thirdness" and so forth;
it does not follow from this that there is any sublation of a second [property]. // 5 //
Therefore, all the aggregates of meanings beginning with the third case, together with the first case,
remain unimpeded in their own places, having been touched by the second case in that same manner.
Regarding that, he says "ataḥ" (therefore).
By the second [member]— that which completes the number two—
and having thus touched it, i.e., having connected it through the relation of opposition (*virodha*).

"Established in themselves" (svasthāḥ) means that, while their establishment depends upon their respective means of valid cognition, the groups of meanings such as the first, third, and so forth, remain indeed uncontradicted by the statement of non-duality; this is the sense. The reading "spṛṣṭāḥ" (touched/affected) is considered possible. // 6 //
But is it not the case that the negative particle (*nañ*) negates everything other than Brahman?
For the mention of "the second" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of everything [other than Brahman]. (7)
Here the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises an objection with the words "Now, [regarding] the negative particle (nañ).
The underlying intention is this: the second word does not have its primary meaning;
rather, it indicates (lakṣaka) merely the phenomenal world of difference (bhedaprapañca).

The negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). "Non-duality" (*advitīya*) is the absence of a second; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of the non-existence of an object.
And thus, the sublation of the manifold of difference is established by the scripture concerning the non-dual. // 7 //

It is not a negation in this way, for from this [statement] nothing other than what is to be known is understood; rather, he speaks here of something else that is either contrary to it or similar to it. (8)
He refutes this by saying "not so.
The particle *hi* indicates a reason:
because from this word "non-dual" (*advitīya*), which is in grammatical apposition with the word "Brahman," it is understood that Brahman is precisely distinguished from a second entity.
But it is not merely the negation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
therefore, the sense is that an *avyayībhāva* compound is not appropriate here.
Furthermore, even this non-conceptualized [state] is refuted here by way of a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*).
That word "non-dual" (advitīya). // 8 //
If it is intended that Brahman is that which possesses no second at all, then the definitions stated as "truth" and so forth would become merely secondary characteristics. (9)
Furthermore, the negation of everything distinct from Brahman is untenable;

for if that were so, it would lead to the consequence that the scriptural passages defining the characteristics of Brahman would become incoherent. Thus he says, "the second," meaning that there is an absence of everything else—that which is distinct from—that with which [Brahman] is connected.

The point is this: if one were to explain the meaning as "that [is] Brahman," then since even the definition—which consists of unique attributes functioning by way of indication (lakṣaṇāvṛtti)—would be non-existent, the statement defining Brahman as "Truth, Knowledge, etc. would become a defective definition. // 9 //
In the case of [the term] "non-dual" (*advitīya*), which has as its scope merely the non-existence of a second object,
there can be no syntactic connection with the word *brahman*, because the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is restricted to itself.

He also states that the *avyayībhāva* compound lacks syntactic connection with the word "existent" (*sat*), by saying "in the case of 'without a second'": in the phrase "without a second," [the compound] is self-contained because it has its own primary meaning as its principal element.
The meaning is that [the word "sat"] is not a qualifier of the other referents. Thus, there would be no syntactic connection as a qualifier with the word "sat," which denotes Brahman;
for this [word "chit"] is a qualifier of that [Brahman] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it.
Therefore, it is not possible to accept that [consequence];
for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable result of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). This is the intended meaning. // 10 //
In that case, the second emptiness is not a qualification of Brahman;
or, if it were a qualification, that Brahman would be either a third or a first [Brahman]. (11)
If it is argued that the absence of a second is indeed the very nature of Brahman,
and therefore its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Brahman" is possible, [the author] says in response:
"The absence of a second cannot be a qualifier of Brahman by way of non-difference."

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is that because non-existence is insubstantial (*tuccha*) and Brahman is real (*satya*), it is impossible for the real and the insubstantial to be identical.
Even if [non-existence] is a qualification of Brahman, we say: the second is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the first;
its state of being the absence of that [second] is the second.
And the third [term] to be qualified is Brahman;
alternatively, Brahman is the first,
and the second is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin).

The meaning of the second half of the verse is that, since "the absence of that" would be the third qualifier, it is unavoidable that Brahman would possess either the status of being first or the status of being third.
Thus, the impossibility has been stated even under the alternative view of it being an *avyayībhāva* compound. // 11 //
Everything that was previously applicable is compounded in a *bahuvrīhi*; and those [words] beginning with the first and third cases of "Brahman" [are compounded] throughout the three worlds. (12)
Because Brahman is non-dual, they remain established in their own nature, uncontradicted;
furthermore, this is so when the compound is understood as a bahuvrīhi. // 13 //
The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which functions as a verbal modifier (*vṛttyartha*), does not connect with another word-meaning (*padārthāntara*).
Only when there is a connection with another [substantive] meaning is the genitive case appropriate, as in the expression "of whom" (*yasya*). // 14 //
Now, he states the refutation regarding the *bahuvrīhi* alternative with the words "prasaktam" (it follows).

Even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, just as in the case of a *tatpuruṣa*, the presence of all [other] categories such as the first, third, and so on, cannot be prevented; thus, it follows as a matter of course. He establishes that very point with the two half-verses beginning with "brahmaṇaḥ."
And as for "Brahman":
in this interpretation, the analysis of the compound is "that for which there is no second. The meaning is that there exists nothing else to complete the number two with respect to Brahman.
And thus, duality would be obtained for Brahman itself.

Consequently, the meaning is that there is no sublation by the scriptural statement of "non-dual" (advitīya) regarding that which is first in relation to Brahman, nor regarding that which is third and so forth.
Being "first" consists in being the completer of the initial number.
It should be understood that being the completer of a number such as three constitutes "thirdness" and so forth.
[The world] is non-dual with respect to Brahman— that is, there is no second entity in relation to Brahman—
and this is because it is either the first in relation to Brahman or the third, and so on, in relation to Brahman.
The phrase beginning with "svasthāḥ" (those who are healthy) is to be explained as before.
Now, one might object: the second member of the *bahuvrīhi* compound must have the meaning of fulfilling the number two;
and if that is so, the relation of inherence (*niṣṭhatva*) of the referent of the pronoun "yaḥ" (which) to Brahman cannot be accepted as a logical connection within that duality.
By this, there is no contingency of [the term] being the first, third, and so on; rather,
the second word has "difference" as its primary meaning,
and within that difference, the relation of having Brahman as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*) is construed.

Since there is nothing distinct from Brahman, that Brahman is "without a second" (*advitīya*); thus, the negation of a second is indeed obtained through the scriptural statement of "without a second. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). For a *bahuvrīhi* compound has as its primary referent a meaning external to its constituent members. Consequently, it must be stated that the absence of a second—presented by the word within the *bahuvrīhi* formation—is a qualifier of Brahman, which is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the compound.
That is not tenable;

the meaning is that in the doctrine of the voidness of everything distinct from Brahman, even the absence of a second is itself void, and thus it cannot function as a qualifier of the referent of the term "Brahman. This refers to the sense of the compound, namely the sense of the *bahuvrīhi*.
Regarding the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which is the absence of a second [entity]:
why is there an impossibility of its connection with another word-meaning? To this, he says: "Because it exists" (*satyatvāt*).
The genitive case in the word "yasya" (of which) is appropriate only when there is an established connection with another entity that is related to the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha).

However, since in the case of Brahman—which is devoid of distinctions—any connection with another category of object is unreal, the genitive determinative compound (ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvrīhi) is not applicable here; this is the meaning. // 12 // 13 // 14 //
The non-existence of a second entity is neither Brahman nor a qualifier;
for that which is non-existent cannot be Brahman, nor can it be a qualifier. (15)

In expressions such as "the head of Rāhu," although there is non-difference, we observe the use of the genitive case; therefore, [the author] rejects the intended meaning that "that which is non-different from the absence of a second is the non-dual Brahman" by the words "dvitīya" (second).
The sense is that it is not logical for a non-existent thing to have non-difference with the referent of the word "existent" (sat), nor can it function as its qualifier. // 15 //
Therefore, the existence of phenomenal plurality is not sublated by the scriptures on non-duality;
it is established by the force of its own means of valid cognition and is even approved by the Śruti.
He concludes the examination of the logical inconsistency of the meaning of the scriptural texts on non-duality as accepted by others with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The meaning is this: the existence of the manifold world of difference (*bheda-prapañca*), which is established by faultless means of valid cognition such as perception and is likewise described by Scripture as having ultimate reality, cannot be sublated by the scriptural text on non-duality;
for, in the manner already demonstrated, the text on non-duality lacks the capacity to establish the non-existence of anything distinct from Brahman. // 16 //
(Thus concludes the examination of the refutation of the opponent’s interpretation of the scriptural text concerning non-duality.
Therefore, this is stated to be the meaning of the scriptural text "Brahman is non-dual" (*advitīyaṃ brahma*):
there has never been, is not now, and will never be anything capable of being counted as a second [to Brahman]. (17)
Whether equal or superior to him, there is no second who can be counted, since this entire world is but a mere fraction of his array of power. (18)
How could it attain the status of being the referent of a second word? Just as [in the case of]: "The King of Chola is today the sole emperor on the face of the earth. (19)
Thus, these words are intended to prevent one from associating with kings equal to him, but they do not prohibit [association with] his servants, sons, wives, and so forth. (20)
Likewise, there are millions of cosmic eggs containing gods, asuras, humans, and Brahmās,
yet [the Lord] remains untouched by afflictions, karma, their maturation, and the like, for He is the Sovereign of all.
They are but drops and mere sprays from the ocean of the majesty and glory of Viṣṇu, who is the treasury of the sixfold qualities beginning with knowledge and whose power is inconceivable.

What, then, is the meaning of the scriptural passage concerning the "non-dual" (advitīya)? To this he replies with the word "tena" (by that). The meaning is that, because the meaning favored by the opponent is untenable, we present an alternative meaning that is well-coherent.

The word "it is said" (*ucyate*) serves as a formal proposition (*pratijñāna*); it is intended to indicate that the matter being stated is as wonderful as something never before heard, and to show that it is worthy of careful attention.
He states that very point with the words "as a second":
when Brahman is first reckoned, there exists no object—whether equal or superior—that is fit to be reckoned alongside Him throughout the three periods of time; this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "In this manifold, diverse, and infinite expansion of consciousness and unconsciousness, how can there be an absence of anyone equal to Brahman?
To this, he says:

"Because... Since even the millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) consisting of the fourteen worlds are merely a tiny fraction of a single portion of the majesty of this Supreme Self, who possesses infinite great manifestations, [there is no one equal to Him].

Since even entities such as *bhava* and *brahman*, whose essential nature and characteristics are limited like those of a gnat in a fig tree, cannot possibly possess even a scent of equality with That, they lack the status of being the referent of the second speech— the state of being denotable by the second word— and thus lack the fitness to be reckoned together with Brahman.
"How would that world attain [it]?"—the meaning is "how could it reach it.

It is intended that, according to our established conclusion (*siddhānta*), both types of verbal function (*vṛtti*) are possible for the term "non-dual" (*advitīya*). And thus it has been supported by the venerable Vedāntadeśika in the *Śatadūṣaṇī*: "But in our position, both types of verbal function are perfectly valid."
By stating the second negative concomitance, the existence [of the probans] would be established as preeminent;
and by stating the emptiness of the second, there is the negation of anything equal to it.
Thus we explain this: in the context of enumerating things according to their excellence, it is logical that Brahman alone should be enumerated first,
because He alone possesses the primary excellence.
For it is observed both in the world and in the treatises that the foremost alone is enumerated first;
indeed, it is well-known among the community of poets that Kālidāsa is counted as the very first when there is occasion for enumerating the host of great poets.
As it is said: "In former times, when there was occasion for counting the poets, Kālidāsa occupied the position of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*)."
This primary enumeration is also accepted by the teacher Jaimini, the author of the Śāstra;
for he formulated the sūtra: "Or rather, the primary [is intended], because of the preceding injunction, as in common worldly usage.
Thus, it is established that in a negative compound (nañ-tatpuruṣa), Brahman alone is to be ranked foremost.
From that, the establishment of his being the foremost among all follows;
and from that, the negation of any superior results.

Furthermore, the second half of the verse by the ancient poets—*purā kavīnām...*—is recited based on the underlying intention that only one who is equal [to him] is fit to be counted as a second: "Even today, because of the absence of a poet equal to him, the ring finger (*anāmikā*) remains meaningful."
Thus it is said: "It became so.
And likewise, through the function of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the negation of equality with Brahman results.

Furthermore, since even for the liberated there is only equality in respect to enjoyment (*bhoga-mātra-sāmyam*), it is not appropriate to include them in the primary enumeration alongside Brahman when the context concerns a principal reckoning.
It should be understood that, in reality, that primary entity is Brahman alone; thus, its non-duality (advitīyatva) is established.

In this way, it has been determined that the scriptural text concerning non-duality (advitīya-śruti) is intent on demonstrating that Brahman is devoid of anything equal or superior, in accordance with another scriptural passage:
"Neither an equal nor a superior is seen" (na tatsamaś cābhyadhikaś ca dṛśyate), as well as: "There is none equal to you, nor any superior" (na tvatsamo 'sty abhyadhikaḥ).

The underlying intention is that, according to the corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇā*), it is logical that the meaning of the word [Brahman] is precisely this, since there is no other being even in the three worlds whose power is incomparable.
Now, he shows that the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) intends the negation of any equal, and provides a worldly usage as an illustration with the words "just as... (*yathā*).
In their previous stage of life (*pūrvāśrama*), these supreme teachers, having defeated the court scholar of King Cola in a debate, obtained from him the royal throne and half of his kingdom.
And this introduction of King Cola here serves as a reminder of that context;
for just as the description of a king’s uniqueness does not negate his royal majesty and so forth, but rather negates the existence of any other kings equal to him.
Thus, he says "tathā" (so it is), meaning that the scriptural testimony regarding the non-duality of Brahman does not negate its manifestation (*vibhūti*).
The word "yāḥ" (which) has been omitted here; [the full sense is:
"those millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) containing gods, demons, humans, and Brahmās."

To the extent that those [other deities] are like mere droplets of water scattered from the great ocean of Viṣṇu’s supreme majesty, they are not contradicted by the scriptural texts concerning His non-duality; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, it is made known by the mention of "Viṣṇu" that the supreme reality taught in the Upaniṣads, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed Śrīmat Nārāyaṇa. // 17 // 18 // 19 // 20 // 21 // 22 //
Who indeed, by merely snapping his fingers, could count the seven oceans, let alone the waves, foam, bubbles, and spray? (23)
"Just as there is only one sun in the expanse of the sky and no second,"—when this is said, it is certainly not the case that the sun's rays are thereby denied. (24)
Just as in the enumeration of the objects to be counted, the number itself is not counted at all;
for there, the number exists separately, like any other distinct object to be counted. (25)
To the objection, "Even if they are unequal, let them be counted together," he replies with the words "ka" (who?).
This is the illustration for the impossibility of counting that which is included within its own essential nature along with itself;
and there is also the illustration of the sun.
Regarding the connection of counting a quality together with its possessor, as in the phrase "just as the primary [is counted]," there is a division:
either as *pṛthaksatī*, meaning existing separately by way of being distinct from that which is to be numbered,
or as *apṛthaksatī*, meaning not existing separately.
The meaning is that [number] is a non-separately established qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).
The phrase "like another object to be numbered" is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*);
the meaning is that when counting the substances to be numbered, the other object to be numbered is counted in such a way that the number, which is subordinate to it, is not counted along with it.
Alternatively, the meaning is that [the subject] is like another unmentioned object insofar as it is something to be enumerated;
thus, its status as a corroborative example based on similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) now becomes appropriate. // 23 // 24 // 25 //
Likewise, by saying, "One foot of his is all beings; three feet of his are the immortal in heaven," he established the entire world as being of this nature. // 26 //

[Objection: "Indeed, all that would be excellent if there were authoritative evidence for [the soul] being a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Brahman and so forth. To this, he replies: "Thus," and "A foot of Him... (*pādo 'sya*).

The meaning is that the collection of Śruti texts, establishing that the world is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman in such a way that the world’s status as a quality (*guṇatva*) of Brahman is proven, demonstrates that the entire world exists as a mode (*prakāra*) inseparably established from Brahman.

Furthermore, this "status as a quality" consists in absolute dependence, which is designated by the term *itthambhāva* (the state of being thus) and is characterized precisely by being a mode inseparably established [from the substrate].
By the term *itthambhāva*, one does not mean a "part-ness" (*aṃśatva*) characterized by being a portion of the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

However, it is indicated that the world's status as a part of Brahman consists precisely in its being of the same nature as the mode (prakāra) inherent within the specific essence of Brahman. // 26 //

Likewise, the supreme scriptures state: "Such is His greatness; yet He is even greater than that. Where one knows nothing else—that is the Bhūman. He creates fear for him who perceives a distinction within it," and so forth. (27)
"For whom this entire universe and world is as minute as an atom compared to Mount Meru"—such [passages] refer to the fact that the whole is of such a nature (itthambhāvatā) as that. (28)
To the question of why the world is not merely a single part of the nature of Brahman, he says "tathā" (so).

By the phrase "etāvān... mahimā" (this much... greatness), it is understood that the world is a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Brahman and a quality (*guṇa*), because it brings about an excellence in Brahman.
Furthermore, the statement "and greater than that Person" indicates the absolute difference of Brahman from the world.
Therefore, it is not logical for the world to be a partial constituent of the nature of Brahman, in the manner that a jar produced by transformation is a part of clay.

Consequently, the intended meaning is that the world's status as a part of Brahman consists solely in its being a portion of a single, qualified reality, by virtue of being an inseparable attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*). This is the underlying sense.
He cites a scriptural passage (*śruti*) regarding the fact that everything is included within the nature of Brahman: "In which," that is,
when that specific Brahman is being fully experienced, one does not perceive any other independent entity,
because everything is contained within it.
That is the meaning of "the Infinite" (bhūman).
It is stated that the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa alone—who is of every kind and whose self is everything—is the Infinite; whereas everything else is merely small.
With the intention that his state of being established in Brahman is understood precisely through the censure of the view that [Brahman] is limited to oneself, he cites another scriptural passage:
"When, indeed, he perceives even the slightest difference in this [Brahman], then fear comes upon him" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad).

The meaning is that when one perceives even a slight interval—an intermediate gap or a severance of connection with Brahman—within this manifold world (*prapañca*), then for one who knows thus, the fear of *saṃsāra* stands before him.
This meaning is intended here by way of the shadow of the opponent's method, in order to demonstrate that the falsity of difference cannot be established from this statement alone.

However, the meaning accepted by the proponent (*siddhāntin*) is that even a brief interruption of the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmaraṇa*)—which is designated as "steadfastness" in the Supreme Self and was introduced in the preceding verse—results in the very occurrence of the fear of *saṃsāra*.
Regarding the world being a single portion of Viṣṇu’s great manifestation (*mahāvibhūti*), there is the Smṛti statement beginning with "of Meru," and so forth.
The phrase "and so forth" should be construed with the words "Smṛtis" that follow.

These [passages] are intent upon demonstrating that the world is a mode (*prakāra*) inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*) from Brahman; they are devoted to establishing its state of being thus. (27–28)
The entire world, both moving and stationary, consisting of a multitude of modifications, is merely a matter of verbal designation;
only the immutable primal cause is real. (29)

Now, one might object: "Even though in the *Virukta* passages the world is established as a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Brahman and so forth, in other passages it is understood that only the Cause is real while everything else is unreal; therefore, in accordance with those [latter] passages, these [former] ones must be considered to have only a conventional (*vyāvahārika*) scope. To this, he replies: "By the word... (*vācā*).
The meaning is that even in other scriptural passages, falsity (*mithyātva*) is not predicated of the manifold diversity (*bhedaprapañca*);
rather, the intention is that it possesses existence (*sattā*) precisely because its essence is Brahman.
This is expressed in such phrases as "merely a modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), which consist of several Vedic words and take the form of a restatement of the Vedic meaning.

The Vedic passages intended to be recalled by those respective words are found in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The modification is a mere name, produced by speech; 'clay' alone is the truth.
Here, the instrumental case in the word *vācā* is used with the intention of expressing the cause (*hetu*) for the purpose [of the modification].
*Ārambhaṇa* means *ālambhana*, which is "touched. The root *labh* (in *ālambha*) signifies both touching and harming; it means, in effect, "seized."
It is called "ārambhaṇa" because it is commenced (ārambhate) or because it is created (sṛṣṭam).
The neuter singular form results from the grammatical rule of retaining only one of two identical words (napuṃsakaikaśeṣa) followed by the treatment as a singular compound (ekavadbhāva).
What is that? It is both the modification (vikāra) and the name (nāmadheya).

When the question arises as to by whom [the clay] was touched, the previously mentioned lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍa*)—on account of its suitability—is connected here as the agent, as in the passage: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay...

The result is that the modification (*vikāra*) consisting of states such as being a pot, and the name "pot" and so forth induced by connection with those respective states, are both grasped by the lump of clay itself for the sake of verbal and practical usage.

Thus, since the causal substance itself assumes various states and thereby constitutes the nature of various effects, the effects are not different from their cause; this is expressed by the words: "Only 'clay' is real."
In this context, "everything earthen" is the subject to be qualified.
The word *iti* expresses a manner or mode.
Everything earthen is established as authoritative precisely by way of its nature as clay.
The meaning is not, however, that [the clay pot] is identical with the nature of clay;
by this, the absolute difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) as maintained by the followers of Kaṇāda is refuted.

Since this statement is intended to establish the proposition that through the knowledge of one, all is known, its purport—according to the direction already stated—is precisely the non-difference of the material cause and its effect.
But this is not the case if only the effect (*kārya*) were illusory;
for if that were so, since there would be no object at all to be known, it would lead to the absurd conclusion that everything is already known.
Or, if "the entire word" (*samastapada*) is what is intended by the opponent, then it would simply be a verbal fabrication (*vāgārambhaṇa*).
It should be understood that the claim that the word *vācārambhaṇa* signifies falsity (*mithyātva*) is itself unestablished and merely an assertion of the opponent's view.

The phrase "that is the truth" (*tatsatyam*) is a restatement of the meaning of the passage beginning with "immutable" (*kūṭastha*). Even though Brahman is the material cause, its state of being changeless is what is intended by the term "immutable."
The Existent Reality is eternally of one and the same form.
[Objection: But if it is changeless, how can it be the material cause?
[Reply: Because Brahman has all conscious and unconscious things as its body, its status as the material cause is indeed established by virtue of being qualified by subtle consciousness and matter.
Thus, this very physical self-nature, which is the eternal abode of both the world and Brahman, has been pointed out by the statement, "All this has that as its essence.
Nor does the lack of transformation of the essential nature render the analogy of clay inconsistent;
for the analogy is consistent simply on the basis of the non-difference between cause and effect.
Now, one might ask: how can there be non-difference between the manifold of the sentient and the insentient and Brahman?
[The answer is: because non-difference is established by virtue of having Brahman as their self (*brahmātmakatva*) and having Brahman as their form (*brahmarūpatva*).

Furthermore, it is said that this alone is authoritative, because of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) within a single sentence: "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
It should be understood that this very meaning accords with the illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntavākya*).
However, following the shadow of the other's [opponent's] interpretation, the meaning was described as: "That Brahman is real (*satya*), eternally of one form.
In the verse, the phrase "merely a matter of verbal designation" (*vācārambhaṇamātra*) means that it is produced entirely only for the sake of prior linguistic usage. // 29 //
The effect is not different from its cause, like sparks from a fire;
this is demonstrated through an extensive variety of examples, such as clay, iron, seeds, and so forth.

Furthermore, since the identity of the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) is established throughout the relevant sections [of the Upaniṣads], the meaning of the scriptural passage "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) is not the falsity of the effect; rather, it is intended to teach that the effect is nothing but the nature of the cause. Demonstrating this, he says: "not different" (*ananya*).

Just as sparks that have flown out from a fire are non-different from the fire because they are parts of the fire, so too the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which has arisen from Brahman and is a part of Brahman, is intended to be understood as non-different from Brahman alone.
And this non-difference has been established in the Śrutis by means of examples such as clay and so forth; such is the meaning. // 30 //
Fire was unable to burn the grass, nor was water able to submerge it;
even the wind was not capable of moving it, except by means of its own power of nourishment.
The production [of effects] has been explained on the grounds that they consist of their cause.
He states "it was not able" because even a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can serve as an indicator of the intended meaning;
this point is well-known from the *Kenopaniṣad*. 31.
"By the cognition of a single primary [principle], everything becomes known"—by such Vedic statements and by the authoritative scriptures rooted therein as well. (32)
"This phenomenal world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, attains its existence through the Self that is Brahman"—this is what is established;
thus, the manifestation of Brahman is not negated. (33)

Now, it might be argued: "Surely you have asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard"—thus the proposition was made that the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is possible only if Brahman alone is ultimately real, and not if many things distinct from it were ultimately real; therefore, even against one's will, the unreality of its phenomenal expansion (prapañca) must be accepted. To this, he says: "One" (eka).

The meaning of the statement "by the knowledge of one, all is known" is as follows: since Brahman is the inner self of the entire universe, is the primary principle of the entire universe, and since everything has Brahman as its body and its very nature consists solely in being a mode of Him, when He is known, nothing remains primarily to be known that is not included within Him. This is the intended sense.

The phrase "and so forth" means that through Vedic statements whose primary purpose is the etymological explanation of meaning, as well as through Smṛti statements that expand upon those [Vedas], it is understood that the phenomenal world (prapañca) has obtained its true nature by having Brahman as its self;
however, the meaning is not that the world, as a manifestation (vibhūti) of Brahman, is being negated.
Regarding the phrase "the attainment of the self as Brahman": it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has the attainment of the self.
The sense is that [the self] possesses the attainment of its own essential nature by means of the inner self (*antarātman*) which is non-different from Brahman.

The reading "brahmatātmalābho 'yam" (this is the attainment of the self as Brahman) is to be considered as the complete text. In that context, "ātma-lābhaḥ" means the attainment of the self—the existence of its own nature—and it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose attainment of the self is by way of being Brahman" (*brahmatmakatvena*). Thus, it has been established by this much that there is no negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which constitutes the manifestation (*avibhūti*) of Brahman, in the scriptures. // 32 // 33 //

If that [worldly convention] were negated, then because everything would be false for both the world and the Veda, all worldly transactions would perish; likewise, even the cognition of Brahman would cease to exist.

Now, considering that the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is logically untenable, and that even the scriptural statements—which at first glance appear to have negation as their primary purport—must be accepted as having a different intended meaning (*anyaparya*), the author, with this intention, says: "The negation of that [is impossible]. If the negation of the phenomenal world were intended, then all worldly and Vedic transactions—including the composition of the scriptures, the teaching of specific meanings, and the adoption of various practices—would be sublated and rendered invalid, as they would lack any authoritative basis.
And they would be non-conformant with reality, because everything would be false; this is the meaning.
If it is argued, "But surely the lack of epistemic validity for conventional transactions involving difference is precisely what we accept," he replies to that with the word "tathā" (so).
The meaning is that if everything other than Brahman were false, then even the knowledge of Brahman arising from the Upaniṣads would entail the consequence of being lost—that is, being unreal.
The underlying idea is that because it would be produced by an unreal cause, that knowledge itself would be unreal and possess an unreal object. // 34 //
The view that perception and the other means of knowledge are not contradictory even though they are false because they possess conventional truth has already been thoroughly refuted. (35)

If it is argued that, although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*) everything distinct from Brahman is false, nevertheless, prior to that, the operation of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth, is established through ignorance (*avidyā*), [the author] replies: "vyāvahārika... (The portion containing this refutation has been lost). In establishing the operation of means and objects of knowledge by means of conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattā*), even the cognition of the Supreme Brahman produced by the Śruti and other sources—which for you is held to possess the status of a conventional means of knowledge—would have as its object merely conventional things.
It would be so; for even the ultimate reality of Brahman alone as devoid of distinctions has its sole refuge in empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*).
And thus, even the ultimate reality of Brahman alone would not be established due to the absence of any means of proving that ultimate reality.
It should be understood that in this matter, the ancient masters and wise scholars have exerted themselves to the utmost; therefore, one should look elsewhere for further details. // 35 //

Therefore, it is established that the world is not sublated by the intellect whose welfare consists in the non-duality of Brahman born from the Upaniṣads, because the world is a manifestation (vibhūti) of Brahman. (36)
(Thus ends the description of the meaning of the "non-dual" scripture, preceded by the establishment of the world as a manifestation of Brahman.
He concludes the demonstration that the scripture of non-duality does not sublate the world with the words "And therefore" (*ataśca*).
Because the world is a manifestation of Brahman, it is not sublated by the cognition of the non-duality of the world and Brahman.
This is because the notion of that very [reality] as being endowed with its manifestations (*savibhūtika*) and yet being non-dual is established by the *Upaniṣads*.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to collect other reasons here, such as its being established by uncontradicted perception;
or else, "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*).
Whether equal or superior, it is that which is obstructed; the meaning is that it is not that which constitutes the manifestation of the world's power. // 36 //
If existence does not exist, how can there be the cognition that "it exists"?
Or if non-existence [is the case], how could there be the cognition that "it exists" with respect to that? (37)
The opponent's position—that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated by the scriptural teaching of non-duality—has been refuted.

Now, in order to refute the view favored by others—that this world is "indescribable as being or non-being" (*sadasadanirvacanīya*)—the author begins an investigation with the words, "But if it were real" (*nanu sattve*).
This is an objection raised by the Mādhyamikas and others: if the world were real, how could it be the object of sublation, such that one could say "it does not exist"?
In this regard, the opponent [argues] that for the Sāṅkhyas and others, [the object] is indeed non-existent;
how then could it be possible for that which is non-existent to be apprehended by a cognition of existence? // 37 //
Likewise, the simultaneous existence and non-existence of a single thing is impossible due to contradiction;
for when there is a conjunction of two contradictory pairs, they each attain the status of being both existent and non-existent. (38)

The Jains, however, have maintained that the manifold world (prapañca) is both existent and non-existent, because there is no certainty regarding the reality of either one of those two [positions]. (39)
Now, the Jains claim that existence and non-existence must be predicated by the force of the cognitions of "it exists" and "it does not exist.
To this, he replies: "existence and non-existence.
This means that two contradictory properties cannot possibly coexist in a single locus, and thus they are not fit to be accepted [as such].
He states the occasion for inquiry with the words "existent and non-existent.

When two contradictory forms are presented, because of their mutual opposition, there arises a lack of determination regarding either both or one of those forms; this is what is meant by saying that inquiry has reached its proper opportunity.
Here, the meaning of the sentence should be stated by supplying the ellipsis: "inquiry is now commenced."
In this regard, he first states the view of the Jains, who maintain the doctrine of non-exclusivity (*anaikāntavāda*), with the words "existence and non-existence.
Their conviction is that there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence in a single locus simply because both are perceived.
Alternatively, this is a restatement of the Jain position, beginning from "attained through the cognitions of existence and non-existence" up to the end of the passage: "the Jains, however, assert."

The meaning is that since there is no cause for determining one between existence and non-existence when both are perceived, people have settled upon accepting both aspects of the phenomenal world exactly as they are perceived;
by the phrase "due to the absence of certainty," the absence of a cause for certainty is intended.
Alternatively, another reading may be possible. // 38 // 39 //

Placing the attainment of existence at the forefront, the Sāṅkhyas have maintained that the proliferation of conceptual construction (prapañca) is always existent, because of the arising of the cognition that "it does not exist."
He states the doctrine of the Kāpila Sāṃkhya, which is opposed to this [view], as "the attainment of existence" (*sattvaprāptim*).

Because negation is preceded by an affirmation and because it depends upon what is already established, the cognition of existence (*sattvapratīti*) is more powerful. Therefore, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is always nothing but existence.
However, their intention is that the cognition "it does not exist" refers to the absence of manifestation. // 40 //

Some have declared that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is inexpressible in terms of being and non-being, by way of negating the aspects of existence and non-existence, for the purpose of resolving the contradiction encountered in the dilemma of the opposing pairs of "existent" and "non-existent. (41)

He states the doctrine of the Māyāvādins, which is opposed to both [the previous] views, beginning with "existent and non-existent. When a dilemma arises—due to the force of cognition—that two contradictory properties, existence and non-existence, would simultaneously apply to a single thing, they abandon both the contradictory properties of existence and non-existence on the grounds that it is impossible for two contradictories to have a common locus. Thus, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is neither existent nor non-existent, but is "indescribable as either existent or non-existent" (*sadasadanirvacanīya*).
The followers of Śaṅkara explain it in this sense; such is the meaning. // 41 //

Others have proclaimed a systematic arrangement [of existence], thinking that for things such as jars, there is a distinction between existence and non-existence based on the differences of place, time, and so forth. (42)
He states the position of the Naiyāyikas and others with the words "existence and non-existence.

The term "by way of distinction" (*vibhāgena*) is used in the sense of the third case (*itthambhāve*). Their view is that existence and non-existence, as perceived through specific distinctions of place, time, and so forth, are established and are indeed logically consistent in the case of things such as a jar. // 42 //
Thus, when doubt has arisen from the clash of disputants, a definitive resolution is made therein according to the doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas. (43)
"Thus, in this way": from the conflict of disputants—that is, from the dispute among disputants; in other words, from their disagreement.
Because of conflicting views and the arising of doubt, an investigation has been commenced for the sake of determining the meaning that is currently uncertain.

The sense is this: therein, after first demonstrating the defects in other positions, the position favored by the Mīmāṃsakas—which holds that existence and non-existence are qualified by limiting conditions (*sopādhika*)—is determined through sound reasoning.
The use of the present tense in "it is being done" (*kriyate*) is due to its proximity to that [commencement].
And this proposition is for the purpose of concentrating the intellect of the listeners. // 43 //
If non-existence were understood as being within the very nature of the jar, then existence and non-existence would indeed occur simultaneously in jars and other such things. (44)
For it is because of differences in place, time, and state that our cognitions arise as "it exists" or "it does not exist" with respect to this very thing at this [particular] moment. (45)

Therefore, the existence and non-existence of jars and other things is established through distinctions such as place and so forth; here, the possibility of the doctrine of non-duality (nirasta-vāda) does not exist. // 46 //

In this regard, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is described by means of three verses beginning with "the nature of the jar" (*ghaṭasvarūpa*), through the refutation of the position that asserts an unconditional conjunction of both existence and non-existence.
The meaning is as follows: within the very nature of the jar, non-existence is indeed perceived;
that is to say, it is nothing other than the perception itself that "[the jar] does not exist."
If he had established its existence as well,
or if he had established that cognition is existence and non-existence without any qualification,
then he would have accepted the conjunction of existence and non-existence.
But it is not so;
rather, cognitions establish existence with respect to certain particularities of place, time, state, and so forth, and non-existence as conditioned by other places and so on.

The meaning is that since existence and non-existence are established in things such as jars according to the distinctions of place and so forth, the doctrine of that [existence] or the doctrine of the other [non-existence] cannot possibly arise, because they are corrupted by defects such as contradiction.
The reading "of the *nirasta* (refuted) *advaitavāda*" is considered possible.

The meaning of this is as follows: there is no possibility for the Jaina doctrine of non-absolutism (*anaikāntya-vāda*)—namely, that "it may be" existent (*syād asti*) or "it may be" non-existent (*syād nāsti*)—once *syādvāda* has been refuted and sublated by contradiction.
And here, the position of the Naiyāyikas and others [is presented].
Then, in the *Śatadūṣaṇī*, the venerable Nigamāntadeśika elucidated this distinction in the sixtieth discourse of his Siddhānta:

"We accept the position that the two [contradictory attributes] are established through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as it is not far removed from the truth. The difference of limiting adjuncts, however, consists in existence by its own nature (*svātmanā sattvam*)."
Non-existence as something other than itself;
existence at its own time, and again non-existence at another time.
Likewise, there is existence in its own location, but non-existence in another location;
here, "existence" is designated as either identity (*tādātmya*) or relation (*saṃsarga*).
In that [first] case, the designation "non-existent" is applied to the very entity by way of a form contradictory to it.

In the sixth position, however, the connection with contradictory attributes itself is designated as the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent" regarding an entity. For a jar is indeed designated as "existent" in its own nature as a jar, but as "non-existent" in its nature as a cloth.
"It exists" means it exists in its own place and time, and "it does not exist" means it does not exist in a place and time that are contrary to its own.
Because it is conducive to perception and because of parsimony (*lāghava*), the elders favor this very [definition].
Herein is the distinction: existence (*sattā*) is characterized by either identity (*tādātmya*) or one of the other relations (*taditarasaṃbandha*).
In the cognition "this jar exists," existence characterized by identity with the jar is apprehended.
Now, in the case of "the jar exists here [in this place and time]," existence is characterized by conjunction with this particular place and time.
Likewise, in the case of "this cloth does not exist," existence in the form of the cloth is apprehended as being characterized by the absence of identity with the cloth.
In that case, regarding the statement "there is no jar here," what is perceived is non-existence characterized by the absence of conjunction with that specific place and time.
Thus, one position is that existence and non-existence, being of the nature of presence and absence, are possible in objects such as jars through the distinction of place and so forth.
Another position is that even non-existence is merely the form of another positive entity.
Just as in the cognition "this jar exists," it is precisely the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) that is apprehended as the existence of the jar;
that very same [nature] is also apprehended in the cognition "this cloth does not exist" as having the form of difference from the cloth.

Likewise, existence itself—characterized by connection with its own place and time—is the object even in the cognition of non-existence in another place and time, insofar as it is the absence of connection with other places and so forth.
Thus, it is established that it is indeed a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) of entities that is the object of the cognition of "existence" and "non-existence.
This very point is also agreed upon by our own school (*siddhāntin*). // 44 // 45 // 46 //
Now, it is argued: "The connection with space and so forth is possible only for that which already exists;
the existence of a non-existent thing is not admitted on the basis of its connection with space and time. (47)
Therefore, since dependence involves two supports, the existence of an existent must always be [inherent];
for it is utterly impossible that the existence of a non-existent should arise through causal factors.
Therefore, the phenomenal world (prapañca), having both a beginning and an end, is included within the category of the unreal;
for it has been said: "That which does not exist at the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the middle.
Consequently, that whose existence is certain should always be understood as being truly real. // 49 //

The follower of Kapila, who maintains that existence is absolute and who seeks to establish both existence and non-existence without contradiction, objects here, saying: "But [regarding] place and so forth.
For it is difficult to establish the arising of existence for a jar or the like that was previously non-existent through its connection with its own place and time;
this is because conjunction, as a relation produced by two related entities, cannot arise if even one of those related entities is non-existent.

And thus, existence [sattva] would result from the connection with its own place and time, and the connection with its own place and time would result from existence; this is a circular argument (anyonyāśraya).
Therefore, the meaning of the passage ending with "existence must always be conceived as belonging to entities" is that existence would always belong to what is non-existent.

[Objection: But if [the effect] were always existent, would it not follow that the operation of the circle of causal factors (kāraka-cakra) is purposeless? Therefore, one must say that its production occurs through the operation of causal factors precisely when it was previously non-existent. To this, he says: "Of the non-existent" (asataḥ).
For the existence of a non-existent thing cannot be established even by a hundred efforts, just as oil cannot be produced from sand.

Furthermore, if that which is non-existent could arise, then because there is no difference in their non-existence, it would follow that just as a pot arises from a staff, a wheel, and so forth, a cloth would also arise from them;
and by some operation, even a horn might occasionally arise on a rabbit.
It is with this consideration in mind that it was said [in the previous verse].
If it is argued that there is no over-extension because the specific capacity to produce a specific effect is restricted to a specific material cause (*upādāna*), we say: not so.
For without the effect being already present within [the cause], even the restriction of such capacity is difficult to establish.
Therefore, one must accept that the effect already exists and is merely manifested through the operation of causal factors; thus he says: "having a beginning and an end."
The meaning is that origination and destruction are simply characterized by manifestation and disappearance, respectively;
the scriptural confirmation for this is found in the words "in the beginning" and "therefore."
The meaning is that it should be accepted as being always existent, since it is determined by its existence. // 47 // 48 // 49 //
That which is non-existent is always non-existent because it lacks connection with being produced, like a sky-flower.
In this regard, there is no distinction between that which is previously non-existent and that which is absolutely non-existent.
(Thus concludes the support for the position that the phenomenal world exists. Regarding the phrase "of the non-existent":
"because of the impossibility of being produced" means because of the impossibility of origination;
"previously and absolutely non-existent" means both previously non-existent and absolutely non-existent.
Thus the doctrine of the followers of Kapila has been established.
It is inferred that the portion of the text following this— which was intended to refute the established Sāṃkhya doctrine, as well as to establish and refute other doctrines— is lost.

For the sake of ease of understanding, the manner of refuting the Sāṅkhya position is here shown merely by way of illustration. Substance (*dravya*), first of all, is indeed eternal; however, the various states (*avasthā*), such as being a pot or being a potsherd, are adventitious.
Furthermore, the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) is solely for the purpose of bringing about a specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*).
Since a substance exists [already], its being the object of causal operations and its undergoing a change of state are both possible.

Moreover, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the restriction of the capacity of each member of the causal complex to its respective effect is established; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the perception of [the entity] as being born or destroyed due to its specific states at various times becomes logically consistent.
However, on the view that the collection of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*) is merely a manifestor, the distinction between a cause (*kāraka*) and a cognizer (*jñāpaka*) is untenable.
If manifestation were distinct from cognition, it would result in nothing other than production by means other than [mere] cognition.
Furthermore, if manifestation were eternal, the activity of causal factors would be entirely purposeless;
if one were to posit another manifestation for that [manifestation], there would be an infinite regress;
and if that [manifestation] were something to be produced, it would entail the consequence of the theory of the non-existence of the effect prior to its production (*asatkāryavāda*).
Since its manifestation is admitted to be a form of origination, it is appropriate to admit its origination exactly as it is perceived.
The doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*)—that the substance itself, undergoing a change of state, becomes the effect while being existent—is precisely what must be preserved.
And this very [doctrine] is also established by the culmination of the three Vedas (*trayyantavid*).
The manifold of differentiation arising from ignorance is false;
its falsity is understood through the scriptural teaching of non-duality (*advaita*).

And because that [falsity] is established as being distinct from both existence and non-existence by means of perception and sublation, it is well-founded—such is the view of the proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādins*).
And it should be understood that this has already been largely refuted by the preceding and subsequent sections. // 50 //
Furthermore, regarding that which was heard in the sixth chapter beginning with Śvetaketu—that "That thou art"—how could there be any possibility of it having a primary (literal) meaning? (51)
Now, in order to refute the Advaitins' claim that only the knowledge of the identity of the self with Brahman as the indeterminate pure consciousness (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*) removes ignorance—

and that this identity of the self with the indeterminate pure consciousness-Brahman is established by the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)— the author begins an investigation into the meaning of the sentence "That thou art," taking up and addressing Śvetaketu.

The *Chāndogya* and other such texts are cited; they consider the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) alone to be the primary authority for the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

[The author] states that even for this co-referential sentence, its literal sense is not possible according to their own doctrine, by means of the words beginning with "of the unimpaired" (*ahatasya*). 51.
The referent of the term *tvam* (you) is the conscious self, afflicted by miserliness, grief, and suffering;
the referent of the term *tat* (that) is the omniscient one, whose will is true, an ocean of boundless bliss.
How can there be identity between these two, which are like light and darkness? (52)
Regarding "kārpaṇya": *kārpaṇya* means wretchedness,
the state of being devoid of a [proper] course of action.
Sorrow (*śoka*) is a mental agitation born from the recollection of past suffering;
suffering (*duḥkha*) is characterized by the experience of present undesirable states.

The intention [of the opponent] is that since identity—established by the use of the same grammatical case—is impossible between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who possess contradictory natures, the primary meaning [of the statement "I am Brahman"] simply cannot be established. // 52 //

Whether the quality [of purity] resides in the object [the Self] or is merely extrinsic to it—if it resides in the object as a differentiator—then the identity of meaning between the words *tat* and *tvam* is ruled out from afar. (53)
"Abiding in the meaning of 'Thou'":
the quality abiding in the meaning of "Thou" consists of ignorance, suffering, and so forth;
and the quality abiding in the meaning of "That" consists of omniscience, being the cause of the world, and so forth.
And that [Brahman] is considered by others to be the "incidental definition" (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) of Brahman.

Since these two attributes differentiate their respective substrates, the identity of the referents of "That" and "Thou" is utterly discarded, just as in the case of a horse and a donkey; such is the meaning. // 53 //
Whether the qualifiers such as "ignorance," "omniscience," "suffering," or "happiness" are intended as attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the element of consciousness,
or rather as incidental characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*),
there would be a distinction between the two meanings [of the word "Self"] due to the transfer of contradictory qualities. (54)
Indeed, states such as ignorance and states such as omniscience are mentioned merely as secondary indicators (upalakṣaṇa), and not as primary qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa).
The meaning is that the single reality is indicated by both.

Therefore, he says "ajñatva" (ignorance) etc., [meaning] there is no contradiction here. Even though [the terms] are used as qualifiers (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the element of consciousness—the reality of the mind—there is nonetheless an identity between the two meanings of the suffix "tvam" precisely because of the difference in their loci (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*): namely, the state of being a *jīva*, which is qualified by ignorance and so forth, and the state of being the Lord (*īśvara*), which is qualified by omniscience and so forth.
The meaning is that it is not established. // 54 //

To claim that the two words *tat* and *tvam* refer to a single individual consciousness by means of breaking off a portion of their denotable meaning—just as in the case of "this is that cow"—is not sound. (55)
One might object: "Surely the primary meaning is abandoned due to contradiction;

however, in the case of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the two words are accepted as having their secondary signified sense (*lakṣaṇā*), just as in the phrase 'this is that Devadatta' (*so 'yaṃ devadattaḥ'), where both words have *lakṣaṇā* with respect to the mere entity characterized by 'that-ness' and 'this-ness'. Thus he raises the objection with the words "vācye" (in the denoted).

"The application of both words to the mere substantive, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), by abandoning the difference in the grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) that constitute a portion of what is denoted (*vācyaikadeśa*), is [done] through *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*.
He rejects this, saying "this too is unsound" (*ityapyapeśalam*).
"Unsound" (*apeśalam*) means not beautiful (*asundaram*).
The meaning is that since the contradiction can be resolved by the indication (lakṣaṇā) of a single word alone, it is not pleasing to assume the indication of two words. // 55 //
Due to differences in place, time, and state, even with respect to a single substratum, there occurs the transition of contradictory pairs; thus, it is appropriate to say, "This is that cow."
He states that even in the case of the two terms in the example, there is no indication [of identity], saying:
"place and time. Thatness (*tattā*) is indeed the connection with that place and time; this-ness (*idantā*) is the connection with this place and time.

Even though there is a contradiction in the connection of "thisness" (*idantā*) with that which is qualified by "thatness" (*tattā*), there is no contradiction in the connection of both [qualities] within a single substratum (*dharmin*).
The connection of a delimited object with two different places is avoided due to the difference in time;
however, its connection with two points in time is established precisely because of its stability.

There is not even the slightest contradiction in the fact that the two base nouns (prātipadika) convey the connection between two places and two times through their identical case-endings, and also convey the identity of the substance (dravya) that is the substratum of those [connections].
It is precisely this meaning that is the intended purport (tātparya) of the sentence "this is that" (so'yam).
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no recourse to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for the two words in the illustrative example.
In the case of the self-luminous element of consciousness, when it encounters contradictory pairs of opposites,
there is no determining factor whatsoever— such as place, time, or state— to establish a distinction.
But you cannot say this; thus he says: "of that which is self-luminous" (*svaprakāśasya*).

In the case of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of distinctions, nothing whatsoever—such as a difference of place, time, or state—is capable of establishing the non-contradiction of the connection between two opposing attributes.
The sense is that because its very nature is self-luminous, even ignorance cannot be suspected of establishing non-contradiction therein. // 57 //
In the self-luminous conscious Self, from which all dualities have been shaken off, the scripture would become devoid of an object, since the delusion of the evil of duality no longer exists. (58)

Since the connection with ignorance is impossible in the case of Brahman, he states that the opponent's preferred view—that the scripture aims to negate the perception of difference created by ignorance and has as its object the identity of the self with Brahman, which is non-dual pure consciousness—is untenable. He says, "shaken off," where the word *dvandva* here denotes difference.
It must be stated that the delusion of difference arises solely through ignorance.

Nor can that [superimposition] apply to that which is devoid of distinctions and self-luminous, because the object to be negated by it is unestablished; thus, it is impossible to assume that the purport of the scripture lies in a knowledge of identity intended to negate such [superimposition].
The meaning is that either the spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*) or the great sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) would consequently become purposeless.

By this, the view that the very distinction within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) produced by ignorance serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) that fashions the states of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) in pure consciousness (cinmātra) is also refuted;
for it should be understood that ignorance itself is impossible in that context. // 58 //

By this [same principle], qualities such as having true desires and being the cause of the world are [superimposed] upon the Supreme [Brahman]— which has *māyā* as its limiting adjunct— whereas sorrow, delusion, and so forth are superimposed once again [upon the individual soul]. 59.

The view that there is no destruction of the individual soul (jīva), which is conditioned by ignorance (avidyopādhika), is the opinion of those who know only a limited Brahman; this has already been refuted previously. (60)

By this [statement], the following is refuted: the distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā* as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), which has been postulated by certain Advaitins upon reflection on the impossibility of the persistence of *avidyā* within Brahman, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); and the resulting distinction between the Lord (*īśa*) and the object of his rule (*īśitavya*), which they seek to establish as being ultimately unreal (*aparamārtha*). This is because such a distinction is not established within pure consciousness, from which all three kinds of difference have been shaken off.
"In the Supreme Lord, who is pure consciousness conditioned by Māyā"—

by "through destruction" is meant that when the adjuncts of Māyā and Avidyā are destroyed by the direct realization of unity produced by the sentence *tat tvam asi*, the state of being the Lord and the individual soul (Īśvara and Jīva) imagined by them also ceases and no longer persists; this is the meaning.
"Already refuted" means that this portion of the refutation has been omitted;
because there is no conceptualizer for those two things intended as non-ultimate, they are simply unestablished.

If [the distinction] were imagined by itself (*svataḥ*), there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If Brahman alone were its imaginer, then because the nature of Brahman is eternal, it would follow that those two [distinctions] are also eternal.

Even if one accepts their cessation through the knowledge of unity (*aikyajñāna*), since that [knowledge] is momentary, there would again be the undesirable consequence of the imagination of those two by the power of Brahman’s own nature.
Furthermore, if *māyā* were the producer of error and the producer of suffering and so forth, its distinction from *avidyā* would be unestablished.

If it were the producer of cognition corresponding to reality (*yathārtha-buddhi*) and were merely an adjunct for the flavor of play (*krīḍā-rasa*), then, because it would not constitute a non-purposive state of man (*apuruṣārtha*), its negation would be untenable.
Moreover, since it is an eternal entity (*bhāva-rūpa*) without beginning, its negation by mere knowledge would be impossible; such objections should be considered.

It should also be understood that because *avidyā* alone is widely accepted, these minor knowers of Brahman who maintain a distinction between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of *māyā* and *avidyā* are [merely] among the non-dualists (*advaitin*). // 59 // 60 //
Regarding the nature of consciousness, whether it be the pure essence or that which is qualified, there are adjuncts such as *māyā* and *avidyā*.
In the former case, there would be a total confusion of all things due to the lack of distinction between the Supreme and the individual soul (*jīva*). (61)
In the latter case as well, if consciousness is likewise qualified, [then it must be understood as follows:

for the nature of consciousness is indeed without division; yet, through limiting adjuncts such as *māyā* and *avidyā*, it appears as if divided and deluded, and thus [in your view] it is considered to be qualified. (62)

It has been stated that the assumption of a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is impossible; furthermore, another refutation is stated by assuming such adjuncts in the passage beginning with "in the nature of consciousness" (*citsvarūpe*).
Do the adjuncts such as *māyā* and *avidyā* connect with pure consciousness alone?

Furthermore, even if [the self] were considered as qualified (*viśiṣṭa*), since it is partless pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the distinctions in its nature caused by the connection with *māyā* and *avidyā* would result in being attributed to that very same [consciousness]; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion between the natures of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). If, on the other hand, it is qualified, what is that qualification?
If it is argued that [the distinction] consists of illusion (māyā) and ignorance (avidyā), then there is the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya);
if it is argued that they consist of the states of being a living soul (jīvatva) and being the Lord (īśvaratva), then there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya);
and any other qualification is simply impossible to define.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) to be divided by either *māyā* or *avidyā*, that which is conditioned by each [limitation] would be one and the same, just as the sky is one despite being conditioned by a pot situated within a hut and by the hut itself.

Consequently, just as the experience of pleasure and pain delimited by hands, feet, and so forth belongs to the single individual soul (*jīva*), so too the experience of sovereignty, suffering, and the like—induced by their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—would result in belonging to the single Brahman alone. Thus, the meaning is that there would be no distinction between the natures of the individual soul and the Supreme. // 61 // 62 //
Do phenomena situated as external bystanders not touch their own intrinsic nature?
For surely Devadatta is not unharmed by the cutting off of the head of a man carrying a staff. (63)

If it is argued that there is no confusion of the natures of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) within Brahman because a distinction of locations based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is accepted, the author replies with the term "taṭastha.
Brahman, when conditioned by Māyā or Avidyā, is called "taṭastha" (situated on the bank).

For one who is established in that [conditioned Brahman], attributes such as omniscience and ignorance would [coexist] just as a person equipped with a staff or an earring possesses those occasional qualifiers like the staff.

The point is that, just as pleasure and pain existing in Devadatta—who is designated as "standing on the bank"—are unavoidable in their connection with Devadatta’s self, so too would they be unavoidable in Brahman.

Since the consequence of [Brahman] being blissful might be tolerated, the author provides an illustration for the consequence of its being subject to suffering, which is intolerable, by saying "for not... (na hi).
Even if there is a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the consequence of the simultaneous presence of contradictory properties (*viruddhasamāveśa*) is unavoidable.
