Without a real distinction between entities, it is impossible to establish order through a mere imagined distinction of spatial locations.
Thus, it is established that the postulation of a distinction between the limiting adjuncts of *māyā* and *avidyā* is futile. // 63 //
The claim that the meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is the state where consciousness alone remains after the removal of the non-conscious portion is also not sound. (64)
(Thus concludes the demonstration of the inconsistency in the view that the sentence *tat tvam asi* intends the identity of Brahman and the Self as accepted by opponents.

By this, the claim that the meaning of the sentence *tat tvam asi* is the identity of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—which serves as the substantive—after discarding the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of *māyā* and *avidyā*, is also refuted; thus he says: "The non-conscious portion," etc.
[This involves] a double figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the two words.
It has been stated by this much that the fault necessarily accrues to Brahman alone. // 64 //
When the state of being non-Brahman and non-self is negated, pure consciousness remains as the direct witness.
The two terms *tat* and *tvam* have as their objective domain the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*).
That primary function of denoting identity, moreover, must rest upon two distinct entities. (65)

Now, he demonstrates that even identity (*tādātmya*), which is the meaning of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) according to the opponent’s view, is untenable, with the words "Not Brahman" (*abrahma*).

Since that which is different from Brahman is not the Self, when the referents indicated by the two terms *tat* and *tvam* are one—the very nature of the inner self (*pratyaktatva*), which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—only that remains.
And in that case, identity, as the meaning of a coreferential sentence, is untenable; this is the sense.
It is inferred that the latter half of this [verse] has been lost;
it would likely have been: "But in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, identity (*tādātmya*) could not possibly exist in pure consciousness alone.
He explains precisely this impossibility of identity in *ekaśeṣa* with the words: "The reality... (*tattvam iti*).
The word "co-referential" (samānādhikaraṇam) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].
That which is its primary mode of application is "that which functions primarily";
this means it has two entities as its substratum.
The point is that identity (*tādātmya*), which is non-difference co-located with difference, is impossible in the case of absolute non-difference.

Here, it should be understood that identity is defined either according to the system of Yādavaprakāśa or the system of the Bhāṭṭas. In the final view (*siddhānta*), however, the meaning of "residing in two things" is that it resides in a single entity while possessing distinct properties that serve as the grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

The distinction is this: identity (*tādātmya*) is understood as the non-difference of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, which is qualified by the difference of its various aspects (*dharmadvāraka-bheda*). // 65 //
As for the dilemma regarding difference and non-difference that you have raised, it is pointless, since bondage does not exist when there is no distinction between the bound and the binder. (66)
[Objection: But surely it is not possible for identity (*tādātmya*) to consist in both difference and non-difference;

for if difference and non-difference were non-different, then even in the case of absolute difference, identity would be unestablished. Alternatively, if there were difference and non-difference [between them], then the same would apply to that as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To this, he says: "Difference and non-difference... [and so forth].
This mode of conceptualization does not exist in the extant portion of the text;
perhaps that portion has been lost.
Is there identity between two distinct things, or between two non-distinct things?
In the first case, it would follow that "pot" is "cloth";
in the latter case, it would be "pot" is "pot"—thus the dilemma of difference and non-difference is to be understood.
[This refers to] one who is non-different from the non-different, that is, distinct from both the different and the non-different.

The meaning is that this alternative constructed by you is purposeless, because it concerns either an absolutely distinct or an absolutely non-distinct entity in relation to bondage—that is, in the absence of a relation of identity (*tādātmya*), which is unestablished.
For co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is never observed in the form "the pot is the pot" or "the pot is the cloth";
rather, it is only seen in the form "the pot is blue."
Identity must be accepted as the very non-difference between those two [difference and non-difference]. Furthermore, difference itself exists between difference and non-difference.
Nor should it be argued that because they are different, their coexistence in a single locus is impossible due to contradiction; for such a claim cannot be maintained.
The sense is that because the blue [color] and the jar are both perceived, there is no contradiction between them;

or rather, the lack of contradiction lies in the fact that while there is difference in terms of their attributes (dharma), there is non-difference in terms of their essential nature (svarūpa). // 66 //
Non-difference, however, is that which sublates difference between two things that constitute its own substratum;
whereas difference is the mutual lack of identity between entities—such is the nature of these two. (67)

Having accepted the very nature [of the entity], he states in two verses that for one who conceptualizes difference and non-difference, there is even a self-contradiction regarding that difference and non-difference, beginning with the words "non-difference. In some versions, the reading is "bhedamardī" (the destroyer of difference).
In this context, the word "iti" (thus) is connected with "evam" (in this way), forming the phrase "ityevam" (in this very manner).
"Bhedamardī" means that which destroys absolute difference.

Having accepted the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of these two—namely, difference and non-difference—the refutation or sublation of the two alternatives of "difference" or "non-difference" is carried out.
By that very admission of yours, there follows an obstruction of your speech— an impediment caused by the refutations you have stated;
"it follows" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
And you are defeated because your statement contradicts your own accepted position; this is the meaning. // 67 // 68 //

The conceptualization of the relationship between difference and non-difference, and its existence or non-existence, is cast aside by the experience of direct perception; it is merely a parching of the throat.
Regarding the phrase "as different and non-different":
does the relation of being both different and non-different exist with the substratum (dharmin) or not?
In the first case, even for that relation, another relation must be stated.
In that case as well, it would follow "likewise," leading to an infinite regress.

If one were to argue that at the final stage an unrelated entity could produce a qualified cognition, such a conceptualization would result in nothing but the exhaustion of the throat and would be contradicted by direct perceptual experience; this is the meaning.
For the cognition of blue in a blue object is exactly the same as the cognition of blue in a lotus.
"This is indeed a blue lotus"—thus it appears directly before us. (70)
Regarding the word "blue": just as the cognition of "blue" with respect to a jar or similar object possessing the form of blue is known to apprehend an inherence in the blue and cannot be denied,
so too the well-known and established cognition of identity with the blue, such as in the thought "the lotus is blue," cannot be denied.

The intention is that the infinite regress is to be avoided either by means of a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that brings about the nirvāṇa of both self and others, or through an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*). // 70 //

Just as, even when the relationship of conjunction is known and within the range of the senses, there arises the delusion of superimposing fallacious conceptual constructions such as difference and non-difference; (71)

Likewise, when the relationship of identity is rooted in both scripture and perception, the delusions of fallacious reasoning and conceptual construction are warded off by the staff of scripture. (72)

He elaborates upon how fallacious arguments (*dustarka*)—which are motivated by an aversion to the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*)—are indeed refuted by perception and scripture, beginning with the words "Just as" (*yathā*).

Regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*), a fallacious argument concerning difference and non-difference is as follows: "Does conjunction occur between two things that are different, or between two things that are non-different?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of conjunction even between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains."
In the final case,
is that conjunction of the property-bearer with itself distinct from it or not?
If it is distinct, there must be another relation for that [conjunction] as well, and for that one too, leading to an infinite regress.
In the case of non-difference, conjunction itself cannot be established;
as for the clear perception of conjunction, the fallacious reasoning, its root conceptualizations, and so forth, which constitute error, result in nothing more than parching one's throat,
and they are moreover contradicted by direct perception.

The meaning is this: just as the identity between a blue lotus and its color is established by perception, so too the identity between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is established by scripture; thus, the conceptualization based on fallacious reasoning and the like is warded off by the authority of both perception and scripture.
The phrase "by the rod of the Śruti" is stated with reference to the meaning of the present subject, the sentence *tat tvam asi*. 71–72.

And the Veda, which is beyond human authorship and free from defects, repeatedly declares with great reverence that "That Thou Art," thereby establishing the identity between Brahman and the individual soul. (73)

He states that there is also the mark of *tātparya* (the author's final purport) in the form of repetition regarding the identity (*tādātmya*) of the individual soul and the Supreme Self, beginning with the words "Nirdoṣa" (faultless).

Identity is to be defined through the difference in attributes (*dharma*) which serve as the grounds for the application of terms, while the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*) remains non-different. In passages such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), this is to be understood by taking the words "thou" (*tvam*) and so forth as referring ultimately to Brahman who possesses those respective bodies, or alternatively, by taking the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth as having Brahman—the Self—as their ultimate referent.

However, according to the view of Yādavaprakāśa and others, the distinction is that difference and non-difference reside solely within the essential natures of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. // 73 //
The liberated self, situated within the lake of the bliss of Brahman, increases in happiness.
Furthermore, because the possessor of the fruit is absent once the fruit has been attained, liberation would not be a human goal (apuruṣārtha);
for if only the element of consciousness remains, for whom would liberation be the fruit? (74)
(Thus ends the description of the impossibility of the meaning of grammatical coreferentiality according to the opponent's view.
By this much, it has been established that, according to the opponent’s view, even the case-ending (vibhakti) does not have its primary meaning, just as the nominal stems (prātipadika) do not.
This is so even though it is possible for mere non-difference (*abheda*) to be the meaning of the identical case-ending.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that according to the opponent's view, the primary sense of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible because the distinction between the properties that serve as the grounds for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*) has been abandoned.

Furthermore, even if only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) remains, [the opponent's position] is not tenable; for if that were the case, liberation would result in being a non-goal for the person (*apuruṣārtha*). To this, he says: "Brahman."
In accordance with the statement, "I have entered this Brahman, as one enters a cool lake in the heat of summer," the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) is metaphorically described as a lake;
for it removes all the torments and afflictions of worldly existence and bestows unsurpassed delight.
The previously printed reading, "the bliss of Brahman resides within the heart" (*brahmānandaṃ hṛdantaḥstha*), is not correct.

The established principle of the scriptures is that one whose self is liberated, submerged in the ocean of the bliss of the undivided Brahman, remains exceedingly and eternally increasing in happiness.
The meaning is that if one were to perceive one's own dissolution upon reaching the state of being the enjoyer in liberation—the supreme fruit—one would not desire it.
This occurs when, through the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa*, only the non-dual pure consciousness remains.
Of what is liberation the fruit— of Brahman or of the individual soul (*jīva*)?
Not of Brahman,
because it is eternally liberated.
Nor does it belong to the individual soul (*jīva*), because at that time the soul itself has dissolved; this is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that pure consciousness alone is Brahman and that this is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the soul, then it must be stated that the state of being an individual soul due to ignorance (*avidyā*) belongs to Brahman itself.
And it should be understood that this [position] is refuted by both scripture and reasoning.

Thus, the collection of objections has been stated against the view that the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is the identity of non-dual pure consciousness, attained through the abandonment of conceptual constructions such as the states of being the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), which are imagined by ignorance. // 74 //
Furthermore, what indeed undergoes transformation into the form of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) within consciousness?
It cannot be the cognition of a jar, because that [cognition] is observed even when the jar is absent. (75)
For it cannot be said that the entire world ceases to exist when that [consciousness] has not yet arisen or has perished,
because such a claim is contradicted by direct perception even in the state of liberation;
nor is there consciousness of anything else upon its destruction, since others are still perceived.

Now, by means of an investigation into the nature of the substratum of the delusion of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) and the cause of that delusion, he demonstrates the inconsistency of the opponent's view with the words beginning "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "It evolves" (*vivartate*) means it appears in a form that is not [its own] true nature.
"Because of perception" (*darśanāt*) refers to the observation of the phenomenal proliferation of difference.

The sense is that because it is impossible for there to be a superimposition without an underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is not possible for the cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth—which come and go—to be the substrata for the delusion of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).
"The world" refers to the phenomenal proliferation of difference;
that is to say, its manifestation.

The phrase "nor even" means that since other distinctions such as pots and so forth are perceived even when the cognition of a cloth has ceased, it is not possible for the cognition of a cloth and the like to be the substratum for the superimposition of the phenomenal world (prapañca).
It is the opinion of others [the Advaitins] that consciousness alone is the substratum for the error of the phenomenal world.
In this regard, it has been stated that it is not possible for cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth to be the underlying substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). // 75 // 76 //
Surely consciousness is one and non-different; no notion of difference exists within it.
For while jars and other objects are differentiated, that consciousness is not, because it is self-luminous.

If it is argued that the cognition of a jar does not manifest at the time of the perception of a cloth, this is not so; for while the jar indeed does not manifest, that [cognition] itself clearly shines forth. (78)
If it is argued that the cognition excluded from the jar does not manifest, [we ask:

is that very same [cognition] expressed by the word "exclusion" (tadvyāvṛtti), or is it something else? If it is the same, then it manifests; if it is something else, we do not say that it manifests. (79)
Regarding this, others raise the following objection:
"Is it not the case that consciousness is one, undivided, eternal, and all-pervading,
while the difference belongs only to jars and other objects which do not appear in the cognitions of others?"
Consciousness, however, possesses only oneness because it is manifest in all cognitions;
the perception of difference within it has as its object only adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*) and does not have the actual differentiation of the nature of consciousness itself as its object.
That very consciousness is the substratum for the delusion of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca-bhrama*).
If it is argued that the cognition of a jar does not appear at the time of the knowledge of a cloth, but rather only the cognition of the cloth appears, this is not so;
for in that case, the jar itself does not appear.
Knowledge, however, certainly does manifest.
If it is argued that the cognition qualified by having a jar as its object does not manifest in the knowledge of a cloth, this is not so;
for the nature of having a jar as its object—which is the very state of being excluded from what is not a jar—is nothing other than the essential nature of consciousness itself.
Therefore, in the cognition of a cloth, that [consciousness] alone appears;
the jar, however, does not appear.

But if it were something distinct [from consciousness], then even when it does not appear in the cognition of the cloth, the appearance of consciousness itself remains unimpaired—this is the collective intention [of the author]. //77 //78 //79 //

Furthermore, for this [consciousness], which is self-luminous and formless, there can be no delusion regarding the apprehension of multiplicity from its own side, except through the multiplicity of objects. (80)

Now, one might object: "If there is no difference in consciousness (saṃvid), then such distinctions as 'this is the cognition of a jar,' 'that is the cognition of a cloth,' 'one has arisen,' or 'the other has perished' would be untenable. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (kiñca).
"Of the formless" means of the featureless;
that is to say, of that which is without distinction.
"The delusion of grasping at diversity" is the delusion of being endowed with unreal forms consisting of diversity.
The phrase "of that which is self-luminous" contains a reason:
consciousness is not manifold because it is self-luminous; whatever is manifold is not self-luminous, as in the case of jars and other such objects.
The meaning is this: even the perception of multiplicity within consciousness is merely an illusion conditioned by the diversity of objects;
there is no real difference within it. // 80 //
Neither the entity nor its property is perceptual or inferential;
even the distinction between objects of cognition such as jars and so forth is merely characterized by delusion. (81)

[Objection: "But surely, even in that case, the difference [between cognitions] must be real, precisely because of the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi), since we observe the arising of relational properties (dharmas) here and there. [Reply: To this he says, "No.
The point is that since the difference between objects is itself unreal, the plurality of consciousness caused by it is likewise unreal.
Furthermore, the unreality of difference is difficult to establish;
for instance, difference cannot be the very nature of the thing itself,
because it is impossible for difference— which requires the apprehension of a counter-correlate for its own apprehension— to have a nature that does not require such an apprehension.
Nor is this a property of the thing itself;
for the difference [of one] from its substratum is a further property,
and the difference of that [further property] from its own substratum is yet another further property.
The same applies to what follows:
thus, the difference from a cloth is a property of a jar,
and the difference from that difference from a cloth is likewise [a property of the first].
Likewise, since that distinction itself would require further distinctions, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result.
Thus, for that which is difficult to define in terms of its own nature (svarūpa), it is likewise difficult to define in terms of its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
For instance, perception (pratyakṣa) does not, first of all, apprehend difference.

Because that which is momentary lacks the capacity to persist until the apprehension of difference— which presupposes the prior apprehension of its own nature and its counter-correlate— and because it is impossible for it to function after having ceased;

and if one were to claim that it apprehends the triad simultaneously, then, as in the case of a cognition with multiple objects (*samūhālambana*), the specific relation [of the qualifier and the qualified] would not be established.

The core point is this: since difference is not apprehended by perception, even inference—which arises dependent upon the apprehension of an inseparable relation rooted in that [perception]—cannot be a means of valid cognition regarding difference.
[Objection: If that is so, then how is difference apprehended? To this he replies: "It is merely characterized as an error. (81)
When that is so, then the arising of the various distinctions of cognition is dependent upon it;
how [could it arise] otherwise, and how much less could its status as ultimate reality be possible? (82)
As for the phrase "when":
the discourse regarding the inherent nature of the plurality of consciousness is far-fetched;
nor is its plurality even adventitious.
Because there is no difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Rather, the meaning is that it is merely an illusion of multiplicity dependent on a difference of non-ultimate limiting adjuncts rooted in the defect of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā-doṣa*).
Thus, it has been stated that the cognition of difference based on a difference in objects regarding knowledge is not in accordance with reality. // 82 //
Furthermore, for that which is self-luminous, the establishment of its prior non-existence and so forth would have to occur either by itself or through another;
however, it is not tenable that this occurs by itself. (83)
Because non-existence is contradictory to its own presence, it cannot persist; and because that which illuminates itself by its own cause is impossible even in the absence of itself.
And because the mind has no other sphere of activity, it does not [arise] from another either. // 84 //

Now, in order to demonstrate that even the cognition of difference regarding [consciousness] is unreal because it arises through the perception of origination and so forth, he states "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) to show the impossibility of origination and the rest.

Having raised the dilemma— whether the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or the posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of consciousness is apprehended by that very same consciousness or by another consciousness— he refutes the first alternative with the word "by itself" (*svataḥ*).
Is its own nature apprehended by itself when it exists, or when it does not exist? He refutes the first alternative with the words: "In itself... and so forth.
He refutes the final [position] with the words "by its own cause" (*svanimitta*);

the meaning is that it is impossible for a manifestation dependent on itself to exist in the absence of a cognizer of itself. He refutes the alternative [position], namely that [it is known] from another, with the words "not other than" (*ananya*).

For an absence must be apprehended by first delineating its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Since one cognition cannot be the object of another cognition, it is impossible to apprehend the prior absence of that [cognition] even by means of a different cognition; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, this argument was advanced even while accepting the position that there is a plurality of cognitions (*saṃvid-nānātva*), yet even under that assumption, the apprehension of the prior absence of that [cognition] remains impossible.
It should be understood that, in reality, this plurality is not what is intended by the non-dualists (advaitins). // 83 // 84 //

Furthermore, since difference and so forth are objects of cognition, it is impossible for them to be attributes of consciousness, just like color and other such qualities; therefore, consciousness is non-dual and self-luminous. (85)
He states the proof for the absence of plurality in consciousness with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The intended inference here is: "Difference does not belong to consciousness, because it is an object of cognition, like color and so forth.
[The word] "therefore" (*ataḥ*) refers to this.

The meaning is that because difference is difficult to define and because it cannot possibly be an attribute of consciousness, consciousness is non-dual—devoid of any internal, external, or similar-class differences—and, due to its self-luminosity, it is excluded from being a mere void. // 85 //
Therefore, the knowers of Brahman understand that whatever has been prattled regarding distinctions based upon those [differences] is merely the play of ignorance.
(Thus concludes the restatement establishing the unity of consciousness belonging to others. "Therefore":

since consciousness is devoid of differentiation (*nirbhedatva*), therefore, as for that chatter of conceptual alternatives such as "Is it the substratum of the cognition of a jar, or rather the cognition of a cloth? and so forth—

The meaning is that the non-dualists (advaitins) consider this doctrine of conceptual construction and the like—which relies upon the differentiation of consciousness—to be the effect of ignorance regarding the true nature of the essence of consciousness. // 86 //
Ah! This instruction on Brahman shines only for those who possess faith;
we, however, are devoid of faith, as we seek logical reasoning. (87)
He begins to refute the opposing view with the word "Hanta" (Well then). The exclamation "Hanta" expresses derision toward those opponents who are possessed by delusion.
Among those disciples whose intellects rely solely on faith and who are incapable of critical investigation, this teaching of yours regarding Brahman may indeed appear splendid.

We, however, being investigators of reason, are not inclined toward faith in this teaching of yours regarding Brahman; therefore, to please us, only valid means of knowledge and sound logic should be employed, and not dry, dogmatic instructions—this is the intended meaning. // 87 //
For cognitions manifest directly, distinct from one another according to each individual subject, just like pleasure, pain, and so forth. (88)
First of all, he says "pratipramātri" (with respect to each cognizer) to show that the plurality of consciousness, established by experience, cannot be denied through fallacious arguments;
[this applies] with respect to the difference between persons,
and even in a single person, with respect to the difference between objects.

The meaning is that, with respect to a single object, cognitions are manifold due to differences in time and differences in instruments; this is established by direct perception for each individual, just like pleasure, pain, and so forth.
The implication is that if one denies the multiplicity of cognitions, then by the same logic, one would be forced to deny the multiplicity of pleasure and pain as well;
if that were accepted, it would contradict experience. // 88 //
For us, there is no difference in the distinctions of relation—such as conjunction, desire, and so forth—which are manifested [by the word];
nor is it accepted that such a difference does not exist inherently or is not perceived. (89)

Now, if it is argued that— just as in the case of space, which is indeed partless, a distinction manifested by its relations is perceived such that one says "this is the space within a jar" and "this is the space within a hut," so too in consciousness a distinction manifested by objects and substrates is not real— the author replies with the word "sambandhī" (the relation).
For example, [one perceives] "this is the conjunction of the ground and the jar."

But that which is perceived as distinct solely through the difference of its relata— namely, "the conjunction of the wall and the pestle"— is indeed a real distinction of conjunction, because it is produced by its relata. Or, for example, just as Caitra’s desire for a jar and Maitra’s desire for a cloth are perceived as distinct due to the difference of their relata, so too each individual desire, arising at its respective time, belongs to its particular person and is indeed distinct.

The point is this: just as there is a distinction between objects and their substrates, so too the distinction perceived in consciousness is indeed real, arising through differences in time and other factors.

In our established doctrine (siddhānta), although the knowledge that constitutes the attribute (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*) residing in each individual person is one and eternal, it is accepted that it possesses plurality and non-eternality by virtue of its various states of expansion for the purpose of manifesting specific objects.
It should be noted here that even though primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternal and unitary, it is like [the case of] the various transformations of that [nature]. // 89 //
If consciousness alone is accepted as being all-pervading and eternal,
then everything would always be manifest.
Or rather, nothing at all, at any time. // 90 //
Thus, by the force of perception, he asserts the plurality of cognitions; and when their unity is proposed, he states the following objection with the words beginning "If" (*yadi*).

If there were a single, eternal, and all-pervading illuminating cognition that is equally connected to all objects, it would follow that all objects must be manifest at all times. Conversely, if some object were not manifested despite its connection with the illuminating cognition, then nothing whatsoever would ever be manifested.
The meaning is that no other cause is possible besides the connection with manifesting cognition. // 90 //
At that time, indeed, no systematic distinction based on proximity or otherwise regarding the object of cognition is possible, because consciousness,
like space, rests upon omnipresence.
"At that time" means the non-proximity of that which is proximate to others.
If the distinction between the appearance and non-appearance of an object were caused by the proximity or non-proximity of cognition, such a systematic arrangement would be difficult to establish.
The meaning is that knowledge is always connected to everything, like space.

However, according to our established doctrine (siddhānta), it should be understood that the presence and absence [of objects] regarding the diversity of objects of knowledge are determined by the contraction and expansion [of the mind]. // 91 //
Nor [is there a difference] through a difference in causes,
because that is absent in the case of what is eternal;
nor [is there a difference] through a plurality of intrinsic natures.
Because of the grasping at that as a unity. // 92 //

He says "nor even" (nāpi) because it is difficult for you to establish a distinction based on the difference in instruments, such that the cognition produced by this particular instrument grasps only this specific object;
the point is that if cognition were eternal, an instrument would be impossible.

Furthermore, he says "nor" (na ca) because it is also difficult for those who maintain the non-duality of consciousness (saṃvidadvaitavādin) to state that there is a difference in cognitions corresponding to a difference in objects. // 92 //
Furthermore, it would follow that the deaf, the blind, and others would perceive sounds and other objects;
and the distinction between teacher and disciple and so forth would result in being without any basis. (93)
(Thus, by refuting the doctrine of the identity of consciousness, the plurality of consciousness is established.

Furthermore, [the author] raises the consequence that the worldly and Vedic order would be violated in the theory of the identity of the illuminating consciousness, beginning with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

Now, even if the illuminating consciousness is one, the removal of the veil of ignorance occurs through the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) projected outward via the eyes and other senses, which is connected to the object.
If it is argued that the established principle— that consciousness illuminates each respective object— is thus maintained,
this is not correct;
for it is impossible for an insentient mental modification (*vṛtti*) to remove the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Or, if that were the case, let that [cognition] itself be the illuminator of the object;
what is the use of an internal excrescence such as consciousness? This has been explained at length elsewhere.
The point is that a distinction between cognitions must indeed be admitted based on the distinction between the grasped and the grasper. // 93 //
Surely, for us, there is nothing whatsoever that is distinct from consciousness; therefore, it is being urged without cause that everything should always shine forth. (94)
The opponent objects to the consequence—that everything would always be manifest—which has been raised by the proponent: "But surely" (nanu).
The meaning is that, since in our view there is nothing at all distinct from consciousness, it is out of place for you to level the charge that "everything would always be manifest. // 94 //
Tell me this, sir: why is it that blue and so forth do not appear? Or, if blue and so forth do appear, why are they not distinct from consciousness? (95)
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) replies with the word "this" (idam):

does this mean that the cognition of blue and so forth does not exist at all, or rather that, because blue and so forth are non-different from consciousness, the cognition of them is intended to be nothing other than the cognition of consciousness itself? This is the meaning. // 95 //
In the beginning, the successful execution [of the Veda] is pleasing to the understanding, since neither words nor word-meanings appear at all in worldly experience and the Veda. (96)
The first alternative is not tenable; thus he says, "In the beginning.

All worldly and Vedic transactions—which are sustained by the cognition of various words and word-meanings—are pleasant to experience and established by uncontradicted perception; [the critique is: these must be properly carried out by you. This is the censure.
"How so?"—this should be explained by supplying the missing words. // 96 //
In the second case, the intended non-duality of consciousness would be contradicted;
for if this manifold expansion of diverse forms were of the nature of consciousness, then that consciousness itself would be of that same nature, and thus multiplicity would necessarily follow. (97)

He refutes the second [position] with the words "the second": the meaning is that if the manifoldness perceived in the phenomenal world were identical [to consciousness], then multiplicity would follow for consciousness itself, which results in the loss of the intended non-duality (advaita). The underlying intention is that one who speaks thus commits the fallacy of contradicting their own established tenet (apasiddhānta). // 97 //

Nor can it be said that because it is a manifestation of ignorance, its distinction or non-distinction cannot be determined; for such a [position], untouched by logic, acts like an ornament made of lac. (98)
Here, an objection is raised with the words "na ca" (nor is it the case that...). The word "nīlādibhidā" (the differentiation of blue and so forth) is to be supplied here as the substantive.

Its inability to be defined either as distinct or non-distinct is due to its being a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, the phrase "bhedābhedānirūpaṇā" means that for which there is no determination of difference or non-difference.

Since this differentiation of blue and so forth is false due to ignorance (*avidyā*), and since the difficulty of establishing [a real distinction] is an ornament when the object is false, the impossibility of defining either difference or non-difference is established. And because it does not follow from such logical possibility, there is no room for the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that "everything would always appear," and so forth; this is the intended meaning. He refutes [this objection] with the words "For that... (*sā hi*).
"Jātuṣa" is a derivative of "jatu" (lac);
by the rule *trapu-jatunoḥ ṣuk*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied along with the augment *ṣuk*.
For ignorance, when touched by the fire of right reasoning, is unable to survive, just like lac.
The intention is that the manifold variety of the phenomenal world will not be established as such. // 98 //
For instance, if this ignorance is held to consist in the absence of knowledge, then because its nature would be indefinable, it could not determine anything at all. (99)

If ignorance (*avidyā*) were something other than reality (*artha*), it would be excellent, since its specific difference [from reality] could not be defined; for it would be illogical to apply to it such conceptual distinctions as "being other than reality" or "not being other than reality. Furthermore, the statement that "this is other than the cause of knowledge (*vidyā*)" is poorly spoken. (100)
He elaborates on the fact that ignorance (*avidyā*) is logically untenable with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
Here, the dilemma is as follows: is ignorance the absence of knowledge (*vidyā*), or is it a distinct positive entity different from knowledge?
He states the refutation regarding the first [alternative] with the words "nirupākhya" (devoid of any designation).
"The state of having a nature devoid of any designation" means having the nature of emptiness (*śūnya*).
And thus, the underlying intention is: how could ignorance (*avidyā*), which itself has not attained existence, be the establisher of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)?
He refutes another alternative by restating it as "a different object" (*arthāntaram*). The connection [of the words] is as follows:

"If ignorance were a different object, it would be untenable"—meaning it would not withstand logical analysis—and it would be impossible to determine whether it is distinct or non-distinct [from its substrate]. Thus, it would be "untenable" (*sādhvī*) because it could not withstand reasoning, and "indefinable as either distinct or non-distinct" (*bhedānirūpaṇā*) because it could not be determined as being either separate or identical. This is the construction.

In this regard, he states the contradiction with his own words: "artha-anartha... and so forth. The expression "well-spoken" (*suvyāhṛtam*) is used here in an inverse (ironic) sense. The statement that "the conceptualization of it as being distinct from benefit or harm and so forth is not tenable," and the statement that "this [conceptualization] is a different object from knowledge (*vidyā*)," are mutually contradictory; such is the meaning. // 99 // 100 //
Moreover, even the existence of a different object for that [consciousness] is imagined through delusion;
alas, if this were so, then ignorance itself would be knowledge from the perspective of ultimate reality.

If it is argued that even the state of being a different entity from ignorance is merely imagined, he says "then" (atha) in response. The sense is that if difference cannot be established, then what you intend as "ignorance" would simply be "knowledge. // 101 //
Furthermore, consciousness is pure and non-inert, whereas this ignorance is not like that;
for what reason, then, is it not determined to be something entirely other? (102)
In reality, ignorance (*avidyā*) deserves to be defined precisely as something distinct; thus he says, "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The meaning is this: why is the difference between pure, non-inert consciousness (*saṃvit*) and impure, inert ignorance—the locus of transformation—not defined as the ultimate truth?

Furthermore, the implication is that since all difference is a manifestation of ultimate ignorance, if the single consciousness were to illuminate all objects, then every [instance of] difference would appear at all times; thus the fault remains as it was. // 102
Moreover, this ignorance of yours, which consists of non-existence and so forth—is that [ignorance] consciousness, or the object of knowledge, or perhaps the knower? (103)

Having refuted the indeterminability of ignorance (avidyā) on the grounds that it is neither different nor non-different [from knowledge], he further states its lack of logical consistency regarding its own nature with the words "Moreover, this...
Let ignorance be either of the nature of the absence of knowledge or of a nature distinct from knowledge.
In that regard, the inquiry as to what the nature of knowledge—which serves as its counter-correlate—is, is for the purpose of critical examination. // 103 //
In its state as the object of knowledge and as the knower, there is no cessation of these two for it;
for without knowledge, ignorance does not cease through any other means.
If it is argued that "it is consciousness alone," then surely its non-existence follows from the absence of [external] entities. // 104 //

Regarding that, he states the defect [that arises] if knowledge (*vidyā*) has the nature of the object known (*vedya*) or the nature of the knower (*veditr*), with the words "if it were the object known" (*vedyatve*).

The meaning is that since those two [the object and the knower] lack the capacity to remove ignorance (*avidyā*), it follows as a logical consequence that knowledge, having their nature, would likewise lack the capacity to remove ignorance.
The word *mate* (in the opinion) is to be understood as a supplement (*śeṣa*) following the word *te* (those two).
He states the flaw in [the view that] it has the nature of consciousness with the words "saṃvideveti" (it is consciousness alone).
The meaning is that because consciousness is eternally established and all-pervading, ignorance—which would have to be of the nature of its absence—is simply not established. // 104 //
Furthermore, whether this [ignorance] is opposed to that [knowledge] or not, it has no possibility of existence anywhere,
because the entire world is pervaded by non-dual knowledge. (105)

Regarding the statement that "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is consciousness (*saṃvit*) and "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is its opposite, he states the following objection: "Furthermore, this... The meaning is that just as blinding darkness, which is opposed to the sun, cannot exist in a place pervaded by the rays of the sun or in the sun itself, so too ignorance cannot possibly coexist with all-pervasive consciousness (*vibhvī saṃvit*) or within consciousness everywhere.

By the term "advitīyayā" (by that which is without a second), it is indicated that even the claim that ignorance is distinct from knowledge is difficult to maintain for the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins). 105.
If you maintain that even consciousness is either non-existent or something other than itself, or even something contradictory,
then abandon at once your thesis of the non-duality of consciousness.
(Thus ends the description of the impossibility of defining the nature of ignorance. He states the refutation regarding all three alternatives as follows: "If [ignorance] were non-existence," etc.
If there exists an beginningless ignorance whose nature consists in the non-existence of consciousness and so forth, [then...]
The sense is that the non-duality (advaita) you intend to establish—namely, that consciousness alone exists—would not be proven.
Now, if it is argued: "We maintain that pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*), and thus our intended non-duality is precisely the oneness of the ultimate;

since ignorance (*avidyā*) is not ultimately real, even though it is beginningless, there is no contradiction to the non-duality we intend," to this we reply: For ignorance, which is accepted as being beginningless, it is impossible for it to be non-ultimate (*aparamārtha*), because there can be no other cause for its conceptualization (*kalpaka-doṣa*).
If that defect belongs to Brahman itself, it is difficult to establish; or, if it does not depend on any other cause, then that defect would follow even in the state of liberation.
Since an eternal entity cannot undergo absolute destruction, its being removable by knowledge is also untenable—this is the general direction of the argument.
Thus, the logical inconsistency of the nature of ignorance has been stated. (106)
Furthermore, to whom does it belong?
If you say "to the living being (jīva)," and ask "who is the living being to whom it belongs?"—well then, this would result in an unresolved circularity of mutual dependence. (107)
Ignorance would not exist apart from the living being (jīva), nor would the living being exist without it;
yet there can be no similarity between the seed and the sprout, because the arising of a living being is logically impossible.
Now, he states the impossibility of its substratum: "And what is this?
That which has no resolution is *asamādhāna*—that which cannot be resolved.
The state of being a living soul (*jīva*) is imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The meaning is that, according to the view that the individual soul (jīva) is the locus of ignorance, the fallacy of mutual dependence—where the establishment of ignorance depends upon the establishment of the soul—is unavoidable and remains unresolved even in the opponent's position.
In our own view, however, because the soul is not imagined (akalpita), there is no fault in admitting ignorance therein;
rather, it is indicated by the use of the pronoun "your" (*te*) that this fault belongs only to you.

The word "vinā" (without) should also be supplied before "jīvādityasya"; alternatively, the reading "narte" is possible. He says "na" (not so) regarding the objection that this fault must be avoided according to the logic of the seed and the sprout (*bījāṅkura-nyāya*).
In the case of the continuous flow of seed and sprout, there exists a relationship of producer and produced between each successive seed and sprout;
however, this is not possible in the present context.
The implication is that it would lead to the absurdity of multiple souls occupying the place of a single soul, and to the consequence that souls are subject to arising and perishing. //107 //108 //
If Brahman is not omniscient, how does it wander about? [To this we reply:
You do not admit that the state of Brahman’s omniscience is dependent upon the notion of a self in the body produced by ignorance.
Because of the scriptural statement regarding its being of that very nature. // 109 //
"Let it be then that Brahman alone is the substratum of ignorance.
To this he replies: "Of Brahman.

The meaning is that for Him who directly perceives everything, at all times and in every way, exactly as it exists by its own nature, the state of being the substratum of ignorance—characterized by various kinds of delusion—is impossible, because it is contradictory.
How can it be consistent with your position that Brahman wanders about?
The implication is that this is impossible because, being omniscient, such wandering (delusion) is inconceivable for Him.
[Objection: But Brahman is pure consciousness alone (*saṃvinmātra*).

Regarding the claim that even his omniscience is false—being constructed by ignorance, having as its object the existence of a manifold of false distinctions, and characterized by delusion—the author says "created by ignorance" (*avidyākṛta*).
After the word "those" (*te*), the word "intended" (*abhimata*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one who is established in Brahman to possess an omniscience rooted in the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which itself has ignorance as its source.

The meaning is that His power is heard of as being manifold indeed, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and being intrinsic (*svābhāvikī*); this is because it is heard [in scripture] to be free from any external adjunct (*ananyopādhika*).
To interpret "intrinsic" as meaning that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of Brahman, on the grounds that [power] is rooted in that [ignorance], is laughable.

Furthermore, it should be understood that if this were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of eternal non-liberation, because the nature [of Brahman] is difficult to transcend and Brahman would thus remain forever ignorant. // 109 //
If omniscience is false because it contains within it the appearance of differentiation, then why should it not be non-false for that very same reason, like another word or the like? (110)

Having thus refuted the notion that [omniscience] is constructed by ignorance, and having also refuted the claim that it is unreal because it contains the appearance of difference—[the word] "tadabhedāt" [is used].
The word "atha" has the sense of "yadi" (if).
"Tata eva" means precisely because it contains the appearance of difference.
"Non-false" means having an object that corresponds to reality.
Through the first and second halves [of the verse], the presentation of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final position (*uttarapakṣa*) is established.
The falsity of difference itself remains unestablished.
The intention is that by this [means], the unreality of that which illuminates it would be established. // 110 //
Just as differences in words, repetition, number, and so forth are the differentiators of scriptural texts,
and just as they possess within them the manifestation of difference [yet] correspond to reality, why should it not be the same in this case? (111)
He explains what was already stated—namely, "like a different word and so forth"—with the words "as follows" (*yathā*).
In the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, the distinction between ritual acts (*karmabheda*) is determined by means of different words, repetition, number, name, quality, and a different context.

These factors, such as different words and the rest, are considered by the experts in the system (*tāntrikas*) to be the differentiators of the scriptures; that is, they are regarded as the valid means of proof for distinction because they establish the difference by virtue of each respective injunctive sentence having its own distinct object of injunction (*vidheya*).

The meaning is as follows: just as the cognitions of the distinctions among objects to be enjoined—which have those [distinctions] as their basis—are indeed in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*), so too why should omniscience, which has as its object the ultimate distinctions among things, not also be in accordance with reality?
If ignorance were possible even in one who is omniscient and eternally liberated, then it could not be removed by anyone, just as darkness cannot be removed from light. (112)
It has been stated that ignorance is impossible in the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, who is by nature omniscient.
Regarding that, he states the subverting argument against accepting it [in Him]: "Omniscient.

Since He is by nature eternally liberated and omniscient, and since He is the Lord of all who stands as the adversary to the ignorance that causes bondage—if ignorance were to exist in Him alone; [then there would be a contradiction].

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence of non-cessation (anivṛtti), in the sense that once one has attained the state—just as the sun, garlanded with rays, [dispels darkness]—then nothing else whatsoever could possibly exist to bring about its cessation.

If it is argued: "But surely, ignorance (avidyā) is removed precisely by the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of the identity of Brahman and the Self as pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is produced by the sentence 'That thou art' (tattvamasi)," [the response follows].
This is not correct,
because a sentence lacks the capacity to produce immediate intuition;
for if ignorance were removed by mere direct perception— as in the case of Śuka and others— there would be a contradiction with the continued experience of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, since the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavāda) will be refuted,

this view of spiritual philosophy— that Brahman wanders about due to its own ignorance while the individual soul (jīva) liberates it through its own knowledge— is contrary to what is renowned among the Vedāntins.

The very exposition of its own nature is the refutation of this doctrine; and thus the venerable Parāśara Bhaṭṭapāda has declared: "May this Rāma-weapon shatter the Kali-era Brahmin-Mīmāṃsakas! Though consciousness is Brahman, it wanders about due to its own ignorance even while blazing.
That living being who has conquered the non-dual knowledge slackens that delusion; whereas those ignorant ones who proclaimed that whatever is perceived is false [have failed]."
Thus [ends verse] 112.
"We see no restrictive rule for the validity of the words concerning non-duality, except for your own persistent insistence. (113)

Now, it may be objected that even the means of knowledge that differentiate [entities], such as the scriptural statements regarding omniscience and so forth—which have as their object the differentiation of things within the empirical realm—possess only empirical validity;
whereas ultimate validity belongs only to the words concerning non-duality.
For the ultimate reality is indeed the Supreme Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions and consists solely of pure Being-Consciousness.

In this regard, one might raise the objection that since even the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is untenable without ignorance (*avidyā*), it must be understood as residing in Brahman itself; thus he introduces the doubt with the words "omniscience and so forth.
He refutes this with the word "regulator" (*niyāmaka*):
there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for such an arrangement apart from the force of the convention imagined by you.
However, the scripture is not an authority for the meaning you have stated.

For instance, since the Śrutis concerning duality and non-duality are respectively intent upon the multiplicity of modes and the unity of the substratum, neither of them can have a false object as its meaning.

Furthermore, the intention of the scriptures on grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is to establish the identity of Brahman—the Self of all—as the indwelling self of all bodies; thus, it is the heart of the matter that one should not admit the existence of ignorance (avidyā) in Brahman that would postulate a state of being a limited individual soul (jīva).
This has been explained in detail in the source materials and so forth; therefore, we shall desist here. // 113 //
Since the states of being the substratum and the counter-correlative are mutually contradictory, how can Brahman, which is of a single essence, be understood as "Being"? (14)

If the substrate is Brahman as inwardness (pratyaktva) and the counter-correlative is Brahman as its [objective] form, from where does this distinction of forms arise? If it is born from the grace of ignorance (avidyā), then since that ignorance also depends upon it, there is once again a mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayaṇa). 115.
He states another objection regarding Brahman being the locus of ignorance in the verse beginning with "āśraya" (the locus).

Here, "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*) takes the form of being the object (*viṣayatva*). What is intended is the contradiction between the status of agent and object, which cannot simultaneously belong to one and the same thing.
Regarding the phrase "mutually contradictory":

the sense is that how could Brahman—which is "Being" (sat), consisting of pure existence alone, of a single essence, and self-luminous by nature—be the locus of ignorance regarding itself, given the absence of any difference in form?
He raises the objection that there is no contradiction due to a difference in form, stating: "by way of being the inner self" (pratyaktvena).

If it is argued that Brahman alone as pure existence (sanmātra) is the locus of ignorance by virtue of its being self-luminous, its nature as "I" (ahantva), or its nature as the inner self (pratyaktva), while as Brahman it is the object— then how has this distinction of forms come about in that case?
If [it is said] it is through ignorance (avidyā),...
There is the consequence of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaprasaṅga*).

The implication is that others cannot say "this [distinction] is intrinsic" for fear of admitting the existence of specific qualities (*saviśeṣatva*). By the word "again," it is indicated that here too, as in the case of the theory of the individual soul's ignorance (*jīvāvidyā*), there is mutual dependence.
(If [it is argued] that because ignorance is not a real entity, this is not a refutation of it...)
But where was this [reasoning] perceived by you as being a refutation of the actual object? (116)
Here, an objection is raised with the words "because it is not a real entity" (*avastutvāt*).

The fact that non-ultimate ignorance (*aparamārthāvidyā*) is difficult to establish is indeed an ornament; therefore, mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*) is not a fault. This is the restatement of the objection in the first half [of the verse].
Regarding the phrase "he avoids the thing":
it is only within the conventional realm of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that defects such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth are mentioned in various places;
however, this is not the case in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
This is because it is admitted that such a thing does not fall within the scope of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*).
Thus, the meaning is that this same fault would necessarily apply to ignorance (*avidyā*) as well. // 116 //
The fault of mutual dependence [arises] from the prioritization of one's own thesis;
it does not follow from being a real entity or a non-entity, and therefore this is not a valid response. // 117 //
"Sasā" [is the reading];
here there is both corruption and a gap in the text.
Whether it be substantiality or non-substantiality, neither is determinative.
Since one would be taking as a reason for the establishment of one's own thesis—that is, an object whose proof is dependent upon itself—the fault of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) would follow.
Therefore, the reply "because it is not a real entity" is not correct; such is the meaning. // 117 //

Furthermore, if ignorance were not [an entity], how could there be an object of conventional usage? Nor is it a non-entity; for if it were so designated, its status as an entity would certainly be established. For by the negative particle (*nañ*) taken as a whole, that which is first negated is an entity.
That [reality] is restored by means of its analysis; thus is its substantiality.
Therefore, it is neither a real entity nor... (*a real entity is neither expressible as existent nor as non-existent*).
(This concludes the examination of the impossibility of ignorance having a substratum. Furthermore:
here several verses are found with many missing portions and are heavily corrupted.

We infer that by means of this synthesis of the perceived fragments, the position that ignorance is neither a real entity nor a non-entity has been refuted here. It should be understood that we have filled in and corrected [the text] according to our own understanding, as indicated by the marks shown within parentheses in the root text itself. // 118 // 119 // 120 // 121 //
Furthermore, tell me this: is this ignorance, which is relied upon and which gives rise to the emergence of conceptual proliferation, only one, or is it many?
And the transmigrating being who has that as his basis is likewise neither one nor many. (122)

Having stated the logical impossibility of Brahman being the locus of ignorance, he states another objection against the position that the individual soul (jīva) is the locus of ignorance, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (kiñca).
The dilemma is as follows: is ignorance one, or is it many? And is the soul, which is its locus, likewise one or many? // 122 //
If that [Self] is one, then that single [Self] of Śuka has already been liberated by the knowledge of Brahman;
therefore, your exertion for the sake of liberation is futile. (123)
(Thus ends the analysis of the alternatives regarding the unity or plurality of ignorance, and the refutation of the position that ignorance is one.
Regarding that, he states the refutation of the position that ignorance is one with the words "If that [ignorance]...
It is indeed a well-known scriptural tradition that Śuka was liberated and Vāmadeva was liberated.

And thus, in the case of Śuka, since the single ignorance that is the cause of the phenomenal world (prapañca) was destroyed by the very knowledge of Brahman, the continued persistence of the phenomenal world is untenable.

Even under the view that there is a persistence of what has been sublated (bādhitānuvṛtti), the effort of moderns like yourself to acquire the knowledge of reality for the sake of further liberation would be entirely fruitless;
for the meaning is that what has been sublated will cease of its own accord, even while persisting for some time. // 123 //
It might be thought: "Vāmadeva, Śuka, and others do not exist for you at all;
since they have been dispelled by knowledge, primordial ignorance is not even mentioned. (124)
For the distinction between the liberated and the unliberated, and so forth, is imagined through my own ignorance;
because it is an object of perception, it is like the manifold diversity of objects seen in my own dream.

Furthermore, as for the statement that their liberation occurred through the knowledge of Brahman, that assertion should be refuted by the same logic applied to the account of liberation in a dream. (126)
(Thus ends the restatement of the doctrine of the single soul fashioned by ignorance.
Here, the opponent objects by means of the doctrine of the single soul, saying:
"It might be thought that there is indeed only one soul."
He alone perceives the phenomenal world as if in a dream;
Śuka and others are like persons seen in a dream.
Even the statement regarding their liberation is devoid of authority, being equivalent to a statement concerning the liberation of Devadatta in a dream.
The intended meaning is that the cessation of ignorance occurs precisely through the direct realization of that reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*).
It is I alone who am called the "individual soul" (*jīva*) as imagined by the root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*);
other individual souls are imagined by my own "cotton-wool" ignorance (*tūlāvidyā*).
The distinction between the liberated and the unliberated is likewise of this very nature; this is what is intended by the phrase "by this ignorance.

Regarding the reading *pratyūhyatām*, the meaning is that his statement—being an action—should "counteract" (pratyūhatām), that is, it should subvert the counter-inference established by the force of the argument concerning the account of liberation in dreams.
The reading *pratyūhyatām* is likely intended;

in that case, the meaning is "let that statement be refuted by means of etymological reasoning (*niruktayukti*). However, the older printed reading, *svāpnam ity ukti-yuktāḥ*, is not correct. // 124 // 125 // 126 //
But surely, by means of such an inference, one establishes the manifold world (prapañca) imagined by one's own ignorance; how then can you respond to another who does not do so? (127)

Whatever reason you intend to put forward for [the world] having ignorance as its cause, that very same reason would apply to that [omniscient being] as well, just as in the case of the proof of an omniscient being. (128)

The meaning is: "If you reject this argument by saying, 'But it is not like that,' then how can another person—who establishes that your own conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is likewise constructed by your own ignorance—be rejected by you according to the same logic?
The implication is that if the reason for his inference is considered irrelevant, then that same point applies equally to your own inference as well.
"As in the proof of omniscience":
if the Sugata is omniscient, what is the proof that Kapila is not?
And if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference in their views?

According to this principle, because of their mutual contradiction, neither of the two is established from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha). Alternatively, just as the establishment of the oneness of all cognitions and living beings would not occur, so too the establishment of everything else—the fact that it is all constructed by a single ignorance—will not be established; the point is that the means intended to prove it is merely a fallacy (ābhāsa). // 127 // 128 //
Thus, since your doctrine is contradicted by mutually inconsistent statements, you appear to be merely prattling nonsense, as if saying "I have a face. (129)

"He ridicules the other's view" means "mutually. The sense is that your doctrine is undermined by the logic of Sundopasunda: you refute others, yet those very others refute your own; thus, you and your followers are like Sundopasunda. // 129 //

Just as the discourse on liberation from a dream is similar to the discourse on liberation from that [waking state], so too is it for you; thus, your exertion for the sake of liberation is in vain. (130)
He states a refutation of this argument by another method, beginning with "yathā" (just as):
"tadvimuktigīḥ" refers to the speech regarding liberation [uttered] by Śuka and others.
It is impossible that liberation—which was not even attained by Śuka and others—could be obtained by you.
Even though it exists, it is like a dream;
thus, the meaning is that your effort is in vain. // 130 //
Just as for them liberation, which was previously non-existent, is said to become existent through the knowledge of the Self, so too [is it] later through the knowledge of the Self.
Let that which is non-existent be designated as "false," even though it appears as existent; moreover, you possess examples from your own tradition regarding things seen in dreams.
He says "just as" (yathā) to establish that liberation will not occur if one abandons the effort for the sake of liberation:
just as it is said that the liberation of Śuka and others was indeed accomplished through the science of the self (adhyātmavidyā),
so too, according to you, that [liberation] which occurs later than that [instruction] is false.
The meaning is that one should not say that [liberation] does not exist in reality merely because it is yet to come.
As for the older printed reading, "sāmarthyābhāvinī," it is not consistent with the context.
To the objection—"But how can the falsity of liberation, which is being produced by my knowledge of reality, be established?"—he replies with the word "santi" (they exist).

The point is that, by the very direction you have indicated, it is easy to say: "Your knowledge of reality does not remove ignorance, because it is a knowledge of reality, like the knowledge of reality in a dream. // 131 // 132 //
Is it not the case that this is not undesirable to me—that liberation will not come about—since, because the self is eternally liberated, that liberation is already eternally established? (133)
He raises an objection, saying "But this is not so," on the grounds that for us, the consequence of the non-existence of liberation is indeed desired;
[the word] "sā" refers to that liberation. //133//

Thus, this summoning of a vetāla at the beginning of rites for pacification and the like would be utterly futile, whereby the labor of acquiring the knowledge of Brahman becomes completely useless. (134)
He avoids [the objection] by way of a jest with the words "this very thing.
The sense is that your proof for the non-existence of liberation is contrary to your own [established] practice. // 134 //
Furthermore, because it is obstructed by ignorance, even though it is eternally existent, it is as if non-existent; therefore, its manifestation is accepted as the fruit of knowledge.
Just as gold and other such things that are already in one's hand may be sought after when forgotten, and just as one finds peace upon realizing that very thing was in one's own hand; (136)

In the same way, due to the non-recognition of the nature of the eternally established Self, the state of being a transmigrating soul is manifested; that state is revealed [as false] by the knowledge of Brahman. (137)
Here, the opponent raises an objection with the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

The intention is as follows: although liberation is eternally established and is not produced by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), nevertheless, the exertion in the practice of the knowledge of Brahman is fruitful solely for the purpose of manifesting that [liberation], which has been obstructed and obscured by ignorance.
Just as in the world an effort for the sake of manifesting that which exists but remains unmanifest—as if it were non-existent—is seen to be fruitful, so it is here. // 135 // 136 // 137 //
Ah, what is this "manifestation" that is claimed to be the fruit of knowledge—a manifestation which resides in the very state of the essential nature of consciousness, which is self-luminous? (138)
Is that very consciousness itself, or am I? What is the nature of the realization "I am Brahman"?
If it is the consciousness of one's own true nature, then since it is eternal, it cannot be a result [to be attained]. (139)

In this regard, although under the view that there is only one ignorance (*avidyā*), it follows that because Śuka’s obstruction of ignorance is removed by Brahma-knowledge alone, the effort of others would be rendered futile;
nevertheless, he states another objection beginning with "Alas" (*hanta*) and so forth.
This [objection] applies equally to the view that there are multiple ignorances (*nānāvidyā*).

Is it the very nature of the reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), which is of the singular form of light independent of anything else, that constitutes the accomplishment to be achieved through knowledge (*vidyā*); or rather, does it mean that the cognition in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti-dhī*)—namely, "I am Brahman"—is the direct realization? [The word] "the cognition in the form of a mental modification" (*vṛtti-dhī*) should be supplied after the phrase "I am Brahman."

"What kind [of cognition] is this?"—thus is the manner in which it is sought to be known. There may be a reading "brahmāsmītīti vṛttidhīḥ" (the cognition consisting of the mental modification "I am Brahman"). The other *iti* marks the end of the alternative. In the first case, the refutation is stated with the half-verse beginning with "yadi" (if). // 138 // 139 //
Now, if the manifestation of the consciousness "I am Brahman" is intended [to be the means], then surely that is itself the knowledge of Brahman; how can it be its own fruit? (140)
The refutation of the second [position] is stated with the word "atha" (now).
*Saṃvittiḥ* means direct realization (*sākṣātkāraḥ*).
For it is not accepted by you that in liberation there exists another manifestation to be accomplished by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
It must be said that that very [action] is its fruit;
however, the sense is that this is not possible. // 140 //

Furthermore, according to your view, that [knowledge] produced by sentences such as "That thou art" would be subject to origination and thus impermanent; consequently, fear would arise even for one who is liberated.
In this context, he states another objection with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

If the manifestation of the self—which has the nature of being eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated—consists of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), then because that manifestation is subject to arising and perishing, ignorance would re-emerge upon its cessation; thus, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one does not transcend the fear of cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*).
This is the meaning.
If it is argued that knowledge, having destroyed prior ignorance, perishes by itself,
and that through the cessation of ignorance there is no possibility of rebirth,
we reply: because an entity that is beginningless cannot be destroyed, the absolute eradication of ignorance is not achievable even through the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*).

However, if there is a destruction with a remainder, then once that [avidyā], which persists in a subtle form, ceases its manifestation, there would follow the undesirable consequence of its re-emergence in a gross form.
Nor can it be argued that even though it is an insentient entity (bhāvarūpa) without beginning, its absolute destruction is brought about by knowledge (vidyā) precisely because it is false;
for there is disagreement regarding its falsity itself.
This is the direction [of the argument]: because the reasoning is fallacious and because the scripture has another intended meaning. // 141 //
Moreover, those who understand conventional usage say that when a sufficient cause for an effect exists, that by which the effect is not produced is called an "obstructer" (pratibandhaka). // 142 //
In this case, what is it that, having begun to arise from its own cause, fails to reach completion because it is obstructed by ignorance? (143)
There is no liberation because it is eternally established;
nor even the cognition "I am Brahman," for [Brahman] is not... [the self].
The cognition "I am" is the abundant cause [of self-identity];
since that exists for the transmigrating being, how could it be obstructed? (144)
Since that [cognition] does not arise now due to the absence of its cause,
and not because it is obstructed, therefore that statement [of yours] is misplaced.
(Thus concludes the examination of the futility of engaging in the pursuit of liberation under the doctrine of a single soul.
Now, he states "Moreover" (*apica*) to show that the opponents' claim—that ignorance acts as an obstacle to the manifestation of the eternally liberated state—is also untenable.
For, by definition, being an "obstacle" (*pratibandhakatva*) consists in obstructing the production of an effect when its sufficient causes are present.
The meaning is this: since liberation is not something to be produced, it is not possible for ignorance to act as its obstructor.

Furthermore, in the case of a transmigrating being during a state of preoccupation with sense objects, the non-arising of [liberation] is due to the fact that the complete causal complex for the direct realization of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra) is simply not present; thus, even in that case, it is not possible for ignorance to function as an obstructor.
The compound *saṃvidapuṣkalakāraṇam* is a *tatpuruṣa* (determinative) compound meaning "the non-abundance of causes for consciousness.

However, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge (*vidyā*), does not act as an obstacle to knowledge.
Rather, when karma—which is the cause for the non-arising of knowledge—is eliminated by means of desireless actions (*niṣkāmakarman*), knowledge is produced from its own causes.

Furthermore, due to the greatness of knowledge (*vidyā*), when the binding karma ceases, the natural, uncontracted expansion of the attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*)—which had its expansion contracted by that karma—is always present in liberation; this distinction must be understood.
Here, opponents might object: "But even in our view, beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) is accepted as the cause of various delusions, which renders the true nature of reality indistinctly manifest."
And when that [ignorance] is removed by knowledge, there is a natural, clear manifestation.
It is precisely because it acts as an obstacle to this clear manifestation that ignorance is designated as a "hindrance.
To those [who hold this view], we say: does its being an obstacle to the clear manifestation mean that it prevents its arising?
Or is it that [ignorance] has the property of causing the cessation of that [light]?

Since Brahman is a clear manifestation, if it were different from the nature of Brahman, it would follow that Brahman possesses attributes; if, on the other hand, it must be said to be non-different from it, then because it cannot be produced, it is impossible for it to act as an obstacle to that [manifestation]. Thus, the first alternative is not tenable.
Furthermore, in the second case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cessation of the very nature of Brahman;
nor can it be asserted by the proponent of the doctrine of attributelessness (*nirviśeṣavādin*) that only clarity ceases while luminosity persists.
Furthermore, while ignorance—which obstructs clear manifestation—still exists, how could there be direct realization?
If that [realization] were also indistinct, it would be incapable of removing ignorance, just like the initial auditory cognition of a sound.
Moreover, the clear direct realization occurs only upon the cessation of ignorance.
Furthermore, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) in that the cessation of ignorance occurs by means of that very [clear experience].

Moreover, if the clear experience arising immediately after the cessation of ignorance did not exist previously, liberation would be non-eternal; if it did exist, the impossibility of *saṃsāra* would result. Indeed, the consequence of the impossibility of *saṃsāra* follows.
Nor should it be said that the very cessation of ignorance constitutes the clarity of the self-luminous nature;
