for since Brahman—which is pure consciousness, devoid of distinctions, and eternally shining as a self-luminous essence—cannot be associated with ignorance, clarity must be admitted to exist even prior [to liberation].

If you argue that ignorance takes its stand there because of its inherent difficulty in being established, then for that very reason, there would be the consequence of ignorance persisting even in liberation, and thus fear would surely remain for the liberated one as well. // 142 // 143 // 144 //

Furthermore, the notion that "the individual soul (jīva) is one" is not tenable according to the actual state of things; for those [notions] such as being a jīva, which arise from ignorance and its association, are indeed false. (146)

The refutations of the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*) have been stated. Now, [the author] states that this [doctrine] is contradicted by perception, beginning with the words "Furthermore, one...
It is maintained that there is either only one soul in the ultimate sense.

Since the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) is false by virtue of being constructed through false ignorance (*mithyāvidyā*), there is no distinction between accepting a single false soul or many, except for one's own dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*). This is the meaning. // 146 //
The apparent unity is contradicted by the very appearance itself, since we perceive [beings] transmigrating by the thousands. (147)

Regarding the statement "there is one soul," does this [unity] accepted [as true] arise from the appearance of only a single [soul], or is its unity extracted through reasoning even though it appears as manifold? Intending this alternative, he refutes the first position with the words "merely apparent" (*prādibhāsika*). The meaning is clear. // 147 //
Until the complete cessation of saṃsāra, the conventional transactions produced by that [ignorance] are perceived as uncontradicted, being distinct from the occurrences in a dream. (148)

He states "āsaṃsāra... [etc. to show that for one who perceives manifold living beings (*nānājīva-bhāna*), there is no sublation (*bādhyatva*) occurring only at the time of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-kāla*), as is the case with the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like.
"Produced by that" (*tatkṛtāḥ*) means brought about by the distinction between living beings (*jīva-bheda*).
"Distinct from the occurrences in a dream" (*svapnavṛttavilakṣaṇāḥ*) means distinct from the practical transactions involving objects in a dream (*svāpnārtha-vyavahāra*).

The intention is as follows: just as the unreality of transactions involving dream-objects is determined within the dream itself by subsequent sublation at the very time of the transaction, it is not so that the sublation of the various transactions prompted by the distinction between individual souls is determined at that same time. Rather, through the very perception of the existence of benefit or harm caused by another soul, an intense engagement in activities corresponding to those [perceptions] is observed—ranging from the wise down to children and cowherds—and this continues until the dissolution of the universe.

Furthermore, even according to the opponent's own system, the distinction between individual souls (*jīva*) possesses only a conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*), because it is not sublated at the time of empirical transaction;
it does not possess a merely apparent reality (*prātibhāsikatva*).

Moreover, the inference that "the distinction between individual souls is false because it appears as such, like the distinction between men in a dream" is vitiated by a logical fallacy (*sopādhika*), since its probandum is absent in cases where the distinction remains unsublated during the state of empirical transaction.
And thus the Sūtra says: "Moreover, because of dissimilarity, it is not like a dream and so forth. // 148 //
Therefore, even the logical unity [of the self] is refuted by reasoning:
"Since their activities differ, it is inferred that other embodied beings have contrary modes of existence; like one's own self, they too cannot be denied. (149)

By the very reason already stated, he refutes even the logical deduction of oneness with the words "by that. By that— that is, because the difference between individual souls (*jīva*) is not sublated during the time of conventional usage—
all souls are indeed myself, because they possess the nature of being a soul, just like me.

The meaning is that the argument for the identity of the individual soul (jīva)—namely, "all bodies have me alone as their self because they are bodies, just like my own body"—is refuted by the arguments establishing the difference between individual souls. Furthermore, it should be understood that the strength of the arguments for the difference between souls lies in the fact that their subject matter is not sublated by empirical experience and is consistent with what is perceived. Now, one might ask: what is that argument for the plurality of souls?
He says of her: "By the difference in activity.

Other embodied beings as well—whose existence is established for each individual self and who possess knowledge, volition, and effort corresponding to their respective [actions], as inferred from the various distinct activities occurring in their respective bodies—are like that [Self] itself, possessing knowledge and so forth corresponding to the activity of their own body.
The meaning is that they cannot be denied.
The mention of "modes of behavior" (*mitivṛtti*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of volitional intention (*saṅkalpa*).

When it is inferred through the inference of selfhood—that other bodies possess a self because they possess movement, like one's own body—the distinctness of those selves from one's own self is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

Since volition and effort, which are the causes for the activity of another's body, possess the quality of being a *guṇa* while not inhering in oneself, it can be inferred that they inhere in something distinct from oneself.
Furthermore, it should be understood that their non-inherence in oneself is easily ascertainable at that time, precisely because one possesses a volition and activity distinct from theirs. // 149 //
Just as the inferences [of smoke] regarding the fire and so forth to be inferred are distinct from one another,
so too are they perceived through direct perception.
Likewise, how could it not be distinct from other living beings? (150)

He demonstrates the illustration (*nidarśana*) for the fact that the selves to be proven (*sādhya*), which serve as examples, are distinct from one's own self, by means of the word "just as" (*yathā*). Just as fires seen in similar instances (*sapakṣa*)— which are the basis for inference and are observed at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— are distinct from the fire to be inferred (the fire on the mountain), so too, at the time of grasping the pervasion that the activity of the body is preceded by consciousness, volition, and effort, [fires] are distinct from the selves residing in other bodies who are the objects of inference.
Why is your own true nature—which is grasped as being distinct from the volitions and so forth that cause the activity of your body—not perceived?
Rather, it is indeed perceived; such is the meaning.
The underlying intention is that the argument for the unity of individual souls is as inconclusive as the argument for the unity of fires, and it is contradicted by direct experience. 150.
If another cognizer were not inferred by means of a specific movement [of the body],
then all worldly and Vedic practice would be destroyed.
The proof regarding other selves has been stated. Now, he states the refutation [of the opposing view] in the words "If not," etc.

For in the world, it is observed that in the bodies of others, social interactions corresponding to those [states] are seen only after one has inferred—through specific types of activity—that another self is favorable, unfavorable, or indifferent.

The meaning is that scriptural conventions, such as the distinction between those who are qualified and those who are not qualified for practice, are seen to be based precisely on the difference between individual souls; thus, if one does not accept the difference between souls, these conventions would be contradicted. // 151 //

Nor can the cognition of the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower be based on a difference due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), because that [distinction] would apply even to one's own body due to the difference between the head, hands, and so forth. (152)
Is it not the case that consciousness alone is one, appearing as various individual souls through association with diverse limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)?
It is precisely the difference in individual souls caused by these adjuncts that accounts for the diversity of worldly transactions and the non-confusion of their respective natures.
Having restated the objection that "even the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is imagined by you," he refutes it with the words "nor is it due to limiting adjuncts" (*na caupādhika*).
The mention of the division of objects of cognition (*meyavibhāga*) is incidental and intended as an illustration.

If one were to accept a systematic arrangement based on distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts, then there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that consciousness delimited by each respective adjunct would be distinct even according to the differences in limiting adjuncts such as the head, hands, and feet.
And thus, there would follow the impossibility of such unifications as "there is pain in my foot" and "there is pleasure in my head," and so forth; this is the point. // 152 //
Just as there is a mental synthesis into oneness when sensations arise in the head, hands, feet, and so forth, so too should that synthesis be for you everywhere. // 153 //
If it is argued that there is recognition [of the self] because consciousness (cit) is non-different even when its limiting adjuncts (upādhi) differ, he replies: "In that case" (*tathā*).
Here, "in that case" (*tathā*) has the sense of adding an undesirable consequence;
or it may mean "just as" (*yathā*).

The meaning is that, in reality, because consciousness (*cit*) is one throughout all bodies, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of experiencing [the sensations of] pleasure and so forth belonging to all [bodies]. Nor should it be argued that the distinction between bodies alone is what differentiates the self, rather than the distinction between hands, feet, and so forth.

Because it is observed that even when there is a difference in bodies—as in the case of Saubhari and others—there is a recognition [of identity], it is impossible for that [difference of body] to be a differentiator [of the self].
Nor can there be a fixed rule that only a body dependent on the karma of a particular person serves as the locus for that person's experiences;
for even the simultaneous connection with multiple bodies in the case of Saubhari and others is produced by that very same karma.
It should not be argued that this is not the case for us [the Advaitins] and others;

for even the restriction of experience to specific individuals (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) would be difficult to establish under the doctrine of the distinction of selves based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikātmabheda*), since the ownership of those adjuncts would depend upon the karma of each self.

Furthermore, since the determination of those actions is established solely by the determination of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), there is a circular dependence; this is the general direction of the argument.
Therefore, the intention is that the confusion regarding experiences and so forth must be avoided precisely through the real distinction between individual souls (jīva). // 153 //

Due to the suffering of hell at the time of death, and even due to the agony of childbirth, the enjoyments of previous births that have long since passed are no longer within the range of memory. (154)

[Objection: But surely, since the self is one even when the body changes, there would be recognition in one life of what was experienced in another life; to this he replies with the word *prāyaṇāt* ("due to death").

It is observed in the world that the experience of intense suffering causes the loss of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), as seen in the forgetting of studied material by one afflicted by a severe fever and the like.

Since there is a difference between births, and because the mental impressions are destroyed by the abundance of afflictions arising at the times of death, hell, dwelling in the womb, and birth, the recollection of what was experienced in a previous birth does not arise in the subsequent birth; this is the meaning.

Intending to show that even the length of time causes the loss of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is said [in the verse] "long past. However, by the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of living, it is postulated that a particular latent impression remains undestroyed and becomes manifest immediately upon birth. Furthermore, it should be understood that for some, due to the excellence of their merit, there is no loss of latent impressions; thus, the non-forgetting of previous births and so forth is indeed accepted in both common worldly experience and the scriptures. // 154 //
When [pleasure, pain, and so forth] arise simultaneously, the substrata [of these experiences] are clearly unmixed; how, then, could there be an illusion of their being a single object? // 155 //
(Thus ends the refutation of the doctrine of a single soul constructed by a single ignorance.
Regarding the word "simultaneously" (*yugapat*):

even when various experiences of pleasure and pain arise at one and the same moment, the fact that there is no recollection—despite the absence of any loss of impressions regarding temporal duration and so forth—is established solely on the basis of the non-confusion (*asaṅkara*) and non-identity (*anekatva*) of the selves.

And thus, there is no occasion for the arising of the cognition of a single self, even though it is of the nature of an error, because the difference between selves is clearly manifested; this is the sense.
The refutations of the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavāda) imagined by a single ignorance have been elaborated [previously]. 155.

Furthermore, this worldly course of life cannot be sustained even by numerous individual souls, each of whom perceives only their own private world as constructed by their own specific ignorance. (156)

Being ignorant of the reports of others and seeing only their own respective dreams, how could they establish that [teaching], which is based on a single common ground such as a collective agreement? (157)

He also refutes the doctrine of the plurality of individual souls (jīva) imagined through various forms of ignorance with the words "nor... [and so forth]. The distinctions between individual souls are imagined by consciousness through ignorance;
and these [souls] perceive the multitude of objects imagined by their respective ignorances individually, as if in a dream.
The core of this position is that other empirical (*vyāvahārika*) living beings are not known by one another;
rather, living beings perceived by oneself are merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), like those in a dream.
In this regard, if one living being does not know another living being—whether empirical or of such a nature—including their qualities, defects, and so forth, then [the following applies].

The meaning is: since there is no possibility of meeting with others and so forth, how could the continuous worldly transaction—which is accomplished solely through mutual experience—be brought about?

By the statement that they perceive only what is imagined by their own ignorance, it is established that they are unaware of anything else, namely, that they are ignorant of the activities of other empirical individual souls (*vyāvahārika-jīva*).
For those [individual souls] are not imagined by the ignorance of another individual soul;
rather, they are imagined by the root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā) alone.
If it is argued that even worldly transactional activity is merely phenomenal (prātibhāsika), then the doctrine of the single soul (ekajīvavāda) emerges.
And the fault in that case has already been stated; this is the underlying intention. 156/157.
Moreover, the self-luminosity, omnipresence, unity, and eternity that you yourself accept would contradict the non-duality of consciousness. (158)

To this extent, the opposing view—that the distinction between the object of cognition (*meyam*) and the cognizer (*mātṛ*) is merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) within pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*)—has been refuted in detail.
Now, with the words beginning "Furthermore" (*kiñca*), he refutes the lack of differentiation (*nirviśeṣatva*) as intended by the opponents.
After the word "those" (*te*), the word "opinion" (*matām*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The meaning is that, by those very properties accepted by you, it follows as a logical consequence that consciousness possesses specific distinctions (saviśeṣatva). // 158 //
Those phenomena are not consciousness itself, because even when consciousness is established,
disputes regarding them are observed.
And due to the distinction between those of such forms. // 159 //

Having restated the objection that because there is no difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), consciousness cannot possess those attributes, [the author] refutes it with the words "consciousness alone" (*saṃvideva*).

Even though the essential nature of consciousness is agreed upon, since Buddhists, Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others disagree regarding its eternality, omnipresence, unity, self-luminosity, and so forth— and because there is a difference in their essential natures— those attributes do not possess the quality of being non-different from the consciousness that is [universally] agreed upon.
The meaning is that this is appropriate for them.
Furthermore, the distinction between their essential natures should be investigated as it has been explained in the *Ātmasiddhi*. // 159 //
Nor are those qualities established by error, such that they would not contradict non-duality;
for those qualities are indeed established by the Vedānta texts which reveal the ultimate reality.
If it is argued that even so, since those [attributes] are not ultimately real (aparamārtha), the absence of a second entity in ultimate reality remains well-protected, we reply: "And not those...
Even for you, it is your own view that these attributes—such as the eternity of consciousness—are established by the final Upanishadic texts as being the very nature of reality.
Therefore, it is unavoidable that [consciousness] possesses distinctions (saviśeṣatva) because of them.

By the phrase "revealing reality" (*tattvāvedaka*) and so forth, it is illuminated that if those [objects] were sublated, consciousness (*saṃvit*) would also be sublated by an identical logic. // 160 //
Furthermore, bliss, self-luminosity, eternity, greatness, and so forth, are held to be the very nature of Brahman; regarding that as well, let this be examined. (161)
Since the non-difference of the nature of Brahman from its attributes is what is intended by the opponent, he states a refutation of that position by another method, beginning with "ānanda" (bliss).
The word "ānanda" here emphasizes the state of being;
"mahimā" means omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
The word "ādi" (beginning) should be understood as including "oneness" and so forth.
The word "atha" has the sense of "if," because indeclinables possess multiple meanings. // 161 //
Is that which is designated as "Brahman" merely pleasure and the other [feeling-states], or do they belong to it, or are they themselves what is termed "Brahman"? (162)
One may conceptualize the view of others thus:
"Is Brahman the mere nature of Brahman, such as bliss and so forth, or are these attributes residing in it?"
Alternatively, there is the following dilemma: does the designation "Brahman" apply to each of them individually, or to them collectively? // 162 //
In the first case, there would be the futility of the scriptural mention of those respective terms in both the Veda and the world;
furthermore, there would be non-difference [between them] according to the previously stated reasoning, [and yet] [Brahman] is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe. (163)
For indeed, having already accepted Brahman, the disputants engage in debate regarding it; thus, by that very act, Brahman becomes possessed of a second [entity] by those very same people. (164)
Regarding the phrase "in the first case":

if there were absolute non-difference, then because the meanings would not be distinct, the co-occurrence [of terms] in passages such as "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*) and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*) would result in being purposeless.
For indeed, there is no co-occurrence of the words "pot" (*ghaṭaḥ*) and "jar" (*kalaśaḥ*).
He reminds [the opponent] that the identity of the nature of Brahman with those attributes is impossible by the words "as previously stated.
Regarding the second alternative, however, he says "in the second [case]" because it would entail that Brahman possesses distinctions;
that very [identity] is indeed contrary to what you intend. 163/164.
In the third [alternative], Brahman would be subject to division at every step because it consists of those [parts];
or else, Brahman would be a collection of them, like a forest consisting of a multitude of trees.
Regarding the third [alternative], he refutes the individual alternative among the two alternatives of the individual and the collective by saying, "In the third":
"If Brahminhood were [attained] individually," it would follow that there are multiple Brahmans— Brahman as truth,
Brahman as knowledge, and so forth.
"Brahman is infinite, Brahman is bliss"—
the meaning is that it is like saying "a cow that is hump-backed, shorn, and full-horned."
"Because it consists of those alone" means because Brahman has the nature of each of those [attributes] individually.
Regarding the objection that "Brahman is the collection of truth and so forth," he states the fault: "that collection.
The printed reading "vināśavat" (like something subject to destruction) is incorrect.

The point is this: if Brahman is the totality of truth and so forth, just as a forest is the totality of a multitude of trees, then since a collection is not distinct from its constituent members, the defects already stated regarding each individual member would inevitably follow; whereas if it were something over and above them, it would follow that Brahman possesses parts and is a quality.
Excellence and illumination are indeed distinct qualities residing in the sun;
therefore, there is no example anywhere where the meaning of a sentence consists of such a division.

Now, one might argue that the sentence "That from which [the world] arises" (*satyādi-vākya*) has for its purport an undivided reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*), because it is a definition of essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa-vākya*), just as one says, "The sun is the most brilliant light by day in the sky, and the moon is such at night"—thereby establishing a Brahman devoid of attributes. To this, he replies with the words: "And excellence... (*prakarṣaśca*).
The meaning is that even the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) does not refer merely to the essential nature of the sun and so forth;

rather, it is intended to demonstrate the unique form of the object that falls within the scope of designations such as "sun. Thus, the sense is that there is nowhere—in any coordinate sentence (*samānādhikaraṇavākya*)—an indivisible, non-dual sentence-meaning consisting of a featureless unity (*nirviśeṣādvaita*) that could serve as a model.
Indivisible—meaning partless. // 166 //

If words such as "knowledge" and "bliss" function with respect to one and the same reality by means of the exclusion of dullness, suffering, and so forth, then that reality does not possess a second entity. (167)
Here the opponent raises an objection:

"By the word 'jaḍya' (insentience), etc., the term 'knowledge' and so forth does not denote a specific property such as 'knowability' (jñānatva); rather, it denotes only the exclusion (apoha) of insentience and the like."
However, since exclusion (*apoha*) is a differentiation, a non-existence, and is merely the very nature of the locus itself, there is no consequence of Brahman possessing attributes (*saviśeṣatva*).

Furthermore, the intention of the objector is that words possess purposefulness by conveying the nature of differentiation whose counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are various insentient objects and so forth.
To this, one should connect [the response] "no" with the preceding argument.
This verse is a restatement of the opponent's position. // 167 //
Are exclusions (apoha) non-existent, or are they existent, or are they neither?
If a sentient being exists, there would be a second [entity] that is real; otherwise, [the world] would consist of insentient matter and so forth. // 168 //
Regarding this, he states the fault by means of an alternative analysis: "Apohas" [are] neither existent nor non-existent; that is to say, they are distinct from both existence and non-existence.
Regarding the fault in the existence of exclusions (*apoha*), he says: "If they exist.
The meaning is that if exclusions were existent, then by virtue of them, an existent thing would become accompanied by a second entity.
As for the refutation regarding their non-existence, he says: "consisting of insentience and so forth."

The meaning is that if there were an absence of the exclusions (*apoha*) of insentience and so forth, it would follow that [the self] possesses insentience and the like. Regarding the statement, "Being is accompanied by being; therefore, it is either of the nature of insentience and so forth, or the other," the printed reading is incorrect. // 168 //
The assertion that [Brahman] is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent has already been refuted;
and if that were the case, Brahman would not differ from jars and other such things.
He refutes the third [alternative] with "existent and non-existent.

The meaning is that it has already been stated previously that since non-existence is established as the exclusion of existence, and existence as the exclusion of non-existence, it is impossible for anything to be distinct from both existent and non-existent.
He states another objection with the words "tathātve" (if that were so).

The sense is that if the exclusions (*apoha*) were of the nature of Brahman and yet distinct from both being and non-being, it would follow as a logical consequence that Brahman itself is distinct from both being and non-being, just like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). // 169 //
Furthermore, if it does not provide a meaning that is contradictory to its own non-insentience and so forth— which are the very things to be excluded—
it could not exclude those at all, just as words with a single referent cannot exclude one another.
He states another objection with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

Without the cognition of a property that excludes [Brahman] from being insentient (*jaḍa*) and so forth, the exclusion from insentience and the like cannot be established by terms such as "Real" (*satya*) and so on, just as it cannot be by synonymous terms for "insentient" and the like; therefore, the capacity to convey an excluding property is unavoidable.
And thus, the conclusion is that Brahman's possession of distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*) by means of those properties is difficult to avoid.
That respective insentience and so forth would be excluded—that is, it would be set aside. // 170 //

But when the counter-positive is perceptible, that cognition which consists merely of another existent is itself non-existence; thus here too, by your own admission, there is the state of being accompanied by a second entity.
(Thus, by establishing the possession of attributes, the claim that consciousness is devoid of attributes is refuted.

Now, it may be argued: "It is not being taught that Brahman possesses distinguishing attributes; rather, through words such as 'knowledge' (*jñāna*), Brahman is taught to have the very nature of being distinguished from insentient matter (*jaḍa*) and the like."
If it is argued that this does not entail the consequence of [Brahman] being insentient (*jaḍa*) and so forth, the author replies with the word "pratiyogini" (in relation to the counter-correlate).

When a fit counter-correlate is not perceived, the mere cognition of the locus itself is that absence; since absence is of the nature of a specific cognition, Brahman possesses distinction (*saviśeṣatā*) through absences—which are of the nature of existence and so forth—that are the referents (*lakṣyārtha*) of words such as "Being" (*sat*), which are themselves of the nature of positive entities.
The meaning is that [a logical] consequence follows (*prasajyate*).
This is stated according to the specific view that non-existence (*abhāva*) is of the nature of a particular cognition;
or else, the phrase "a cognition of merely another entity" culminates in the sense of "another entity being perceived."

The meaning is as follows: when a counter-positive (pratiyogin) is not perceived in its appropriate locus, whatever other positive entity (bhāvāntara) is perceived in that locus receives the designation "absence" (abhāva) in relation to that counter-positive; thus, because absences consist of a distinct property (dharmāntara) residing in the locus, it follows that they possess specific qualifications (saviśeṣatva).
Non-existence in a substance is a property (dharma). However, because a property brings about its own and others' manifestation, its very nature (svarūpa) is non-existence;
or, when possible, it is another property—this is the established rule according to how it is perceived.
When something is perceived such that the superimposition of anything else is no longer possible,
that very thing possesses the nature of the absence of those others.

However, since the superimposition of differences occurs precisely while the positive essence (*satsvarūpa*) is being perceived, it is impossible for that [positive essence] to have the nature of the absence of others.

It should not be argued that the delusion of difference occurs when [reality] appears indistinctly due to ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas it does not occur when [reality] appears distinctly upon the cessation of ignorance; for thus, the distinct nature would be of the form of a non-existence. This is because if distinctness were the very nature [of reality], then even previously, the superimposition of differences such as ignorance would be impossible.
For if it were distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it would follow that only that [distinction] would be of the nature of non-existence, and not the essential nature itself.
Furthermore, in the case of an object that is devoid of attributes and self-luminous, it is impossible to speak of either clear or indistinct manifestation.
However, in the case of an object possessing attributes, manifestation through only a few forms is what is meant by "indistinct."
The distinction is that its manifestation in all modes is clear.
Furthermore, if Brahman were a substance, it would possess attributes;
however, if it were not a substance, it would follow that it must be of the nature of some attribute belonging to something else.
In this context, it should be considered that the claim of being distinct from both substance and non-substance is not possible;

furthermore, by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "here too," it is indicated that even if one resorts to the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of exclusion (*apoha*) for words such as "real" (*satya*), the establishment of featurelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*) is not achieved,
and that the very effort of conceiving such a figurative indication is particularly problematic.
Thus, the indeterminability—being neither existent nor non-existent—of even those things such as reality which consist of the nature of exclusion (apoha) has been refuted. // 171 //

From what is it determined that the distinctions between primary elements and their derivatives are distinct from both existence and non-existence—is it through perception and the other means of knowledge, or rather from scripture? (172)
To the extent that the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, arise by delimiting their respective objects according to their particular natures, that much is self-evident. (173)

Now, by means of the words beginning with "bhūte," [the author] refutes the position of others—that even the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indescribable as being either existent or non-existent—due to the same logical consequence.
Regarding the phrase "perception and so forth":

it is well known that perception and the other means of valid cognition make their respective objects of knowledge understood, each according to its own specific form, as distinguished from other things of the same or different classes.

The meaning is that these means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) establish the very existence of things by way of their specific, unique forms; it is not, however, that they establish an indefinability as either existent or non-existent. // 172 // 173 //
Just as when a blue object stands before one, there is no discussion of other colors, and the cognition has a single form; for the perception of a white crystal is not like that.
Just as the perception of sweetness in milk is not at all the perception of bitterness, so too are all worldly and Vedic conventional practices fixed. (175)
He establishes this very point with the words "just as":
the cognition of blue regarding a blue object and the cognition of white regarding a crystal do not have a single object.
Rather, it has as its object qualities that are mutually exclusive;
thus, there is the cognition of sweetness in milk and the cognition of astringency in the neem tree.
Thus, the point is that it is established that cognitions have distinct objects as their objective supports.
In the case of blue, the cognition of blue has a single form and a single object;
therefore, in that blue, there is no contingency of other qualities such as "non-blue" arising.
The term *dhavalamati* is distinguished from that [previous one], meaning it has a different form;
either the word *tādṛk* (such) is supplied after *naiva*,
or the reading may be *naivam* (not so).

Having stated that there is uncontradicted cognition regarding the distinctness of the unique forms of various objects, he also presents a corresponding linguistic usage as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by saying, "linguistic usages are [the basis of] valid knowledge.

The underlying sense is that, by the force of uncontradicted means of valid knowledge such as perception and the linguistic usages rooted therein, one must accept that things exist precisely through their respective unique forms. // 174 // 175 //
If it is argued that this [cognition] has truth as its basis and no other, that is not so;
for if it exists, let its basis be postulated by means of its being an effect. (176)
The doubt is restated as "It is true. He refutes it with "Not so," the word "well" being understood as the ellipsis.
The sense is that, by the force of the effect, one should infer a corresponding root that establishes the reality of those uncontradicted cognitions. // 176 //

And the sense-faculties, the inferential marks, and so forth, are established [as distinct] because they follow the existence of those [objects], since simultaneous occurrence and sequential occurrence are impossible for both exclusion and affirmation. (177)
And as for the delusion that difference is not perceived because of the impossibility of their being one—that arises from the failure to distinguish between difference and mutual non-existence. (178)

He says "established" (*klptam*) because the fact that only non-defective sense organs and so forth are the cause for the truthfulness of a cognition is proven by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and thus it cannot be denied;
the meaning is that the distinction between objects is grasped solely by the means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) in the form of unimpaired senses.
Here, he raises an objection with the words "simultaneity" (*yaugapadya*).
Exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is the apprehension of difference;
affirmation (*vidhāna*) is the apprehension of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*).
It is not possible for perceptual cognition to simultaneously grasp both the locus and the difference residing therein.

Because the apprehension of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is independent of the apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas the apprehension of difference (*bheda*) is dependent upon it; furthermore,
the sequence— first grasping the nature of the locus and then grasping the difference— is also impossible.
Because cognition is momentary, it is impossible for it to function by pausing;
furthermore, the identity of the distinct natures [of the object and the cognition], as well as the identity of their respective apprehensions, is not possible.
Therefore, the apprehension of the nature [of the object] alone constitutes the form of perceptual valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramiti*).
The point is that the apprehension of difference is indeed characterized by error.
He rejects this doubt with the words "this" (imām) and so forth.
Difference (*bheda*) is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is the absence of connection of one thing with another; or rather, it is difference—the distinction between types of non-existence such as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth. Mutual non-existence is difference.
The meaning is that the aforementioned delusion of others is caused by their ignorance regarding the true nature and reality of those two. // 177 // 178 //
The very nature of entities, as it flashes forth in direct perception,
may serve as the cause for the linguistic expression of difference in dependence upon a counter-correlate.
He first states the true nature of difference, saying "the very own-form" (*svarūpam eva*).
"Own-form" means its own unique characteristic (*svāsādhāraṇākāra*).

That very form, when being perceived, becomes the cause for the linguistic usage of "difference from another" through the auxiliary condition of the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
The meaning is that, for example, the very possession of a shell-like neck and so forth constitutes the difference of a jar from a cloth. // 179 //
Just as the cognition of "mere-ness" establishes various verbal designations, or just as the distinctions of shortness and length exist in a single six-fingered object. (180)

The meaning is as follows: "an illustration here is as follows" means that, for those who maintain that non-existence (abhāva) is the very nature of its locus, the cognition of the true nature of the ground itself— when there is no perception of a jar or the like— is held to be the means of establishing the conventional usage of the "emptiness of a jar," provided it is assisted by the recollection of that [jar].

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, the distinction is that difference (*bheda*) and so forth are essentially specific properties residing in a locus (*adhikaraṇavṛttidharmaviśeṣarūpatva*).

He confirms, by way of illustration, how a single entity alone can serve as the basis for various linguistic usages through the difference of its correlates, starting with the word "short" (*hrasve*).
In a single object measuring six finger-breadths, there is the usage of "long" in relation to something else, such as a foot, and the usage of "short" in relation to another object.

The meaning is this: it is precisely the cognition of that object which, depending upon the short [object], produces the conventional usage of "long" through the assistance of the recollection of its respective counter-correlate. // 180 //
Thus, because the manifold world of direct perception possesses many established varieties of forms, its existence cannot be denied. (181)
Thus it is said:

since the apprehension of difference, which is characterized by its own nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), is possible at the very first moment of grasping the locus (*dharmī*), and because the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is required only for the linguistic usage of difference, the reality of the nature of various objects distinguished by their multiple forms is established by the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).
The sense is that it is not something that can be denied.
Since difference, which consists of a unique form, is self-establishing (svaparanirvāhaka), there is no infinite regress (anavasthā).
Its prior non-existence (tatprāgabhāva) is of the nature of its preceding state.
Destruction is the nature of the state following that [destruction].
Absolute non-existence consists in a specific nature of the locus itself. These are occasional absences (*sāmayikābhāva*).
It consists of the very nature of each respective locus as delimited by a specific time.

Furthermore, it should be understood here that while these [absences] are manifested in linguistic usage through their being colored by their respective counter-correlates, they require the recollection of those respective counter-correlates for such usage; this is the distinction to be grasped. // 181 //
Scripture, because it culminates in action, is not a means of valid cognition regarding such a matter;
even if it were authoritative, it would not convey [the meaning], as its constituent words lack syntactic compatibility.

Thus, it has been established that perception alone is the means of valid cognition regarding the existence of the manifold of difference (*bheda-prapañca*), and not its being "indefinable as existent or non-existent" (*sadasad-anirvacanīyatva*).
He states [the following] with the words "scripture" (*āgama*) to show that even scripture lacks authority on this point.
Scripture (*āgama*) is the treatise (*śāstra*), because it culminates in action— that is, because it is intent upon establishing the meaning of what is to be done—
with respect to such matters as the unreality and indeterminability of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which do not pertain to what is to be accomplished.
"Not valid"—that is, "not a means of valid cognition. This is according to the Mīmāṃsaka view.
According to the Siddhāntin's view as well, he says: "even if it were a means of valid cognition."

The meaning is this: even though the treatise possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its established subject matter (*siddhārtha*), the mere word "valid means of knowledge" does not apply to [concepts such as] "inexplicability" (*anirvacanīyatva*) and the like;

for statements such as "neither existent nor non-existent" do not produce verbal cognition because their meanings are incoherent. The underlying intention is that even a composition which appears to convey such [contradictory] things must be interpreted as having a non-contradictory purpose. 182.
Since it is not perceived as non-existent and since it is sublated, it is not existent either;
yet, why is it not existent simply because it is perceived?
If the world were non-existent due to sublation, from where would it arise?
Therefore, you have resorted to this very ignorance through ignorance itself. // 183 //

Now, he states that inference (*anumāna*) also lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) if it is itself indescribable as being either existent or non-existent, with the words "not non-existent" (*nāsad*).
The reasoning—that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent because it is perceived while being sublated—is itself not real;

for the argument that "the world possesses both existence and non-existence for that very reason" shares the same logical vulnerability as a fallacious appearance (*ābhāsa*). This is the intended meaning.
The contradiction intended here is between absolute existence and absolute non-existence, which are devoid of limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*).

Therefore, since indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) is not established, the postulation of ignorance (*avidyā*) as its cause is merely the product of your own ignorance; this is the meaning. // 183 //
Furthermore, the property of the manifold of difference is characterized by falsity; it must be either false or ultimate reality. This first alternative is not correct. (184)

If that [duality] were false, the reality of the phenomenal world (prapañca) would be impossible to deny; even if it were ultimately real, your non-dualism (advaita) would be destroyed by that very fact. (185)
(Thus ends the refutation of the falsity of the phenomenal world as consisting in its being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent.

Furthermore, he refutes in another way the falsity consisting in the world's being "indefinable as either existent or non-existent" because it is undermined by the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), stating: "Moreover...
If the falsity of difference itself were false, then the reality of difference would be established.

The meaning is that if the falsity of difference were itself real, then one would have to admit the reality of something distinct from Brahman, which would constitute an abandonment of the established tenet (*apasiddhānta*) and a contradiction of non-duality (*advaita*).
Nor should it be argued that the falsity of difference is real and is simply the very nature of Brahman, and thus there is no loss of non-duality and so forth.
If that were the case, it would follow that Brahman possesses the quality of being a false entity; the details of this are explained elsewhere. // 184 // 185 //
All means of valid cognition indeed manifest by excluding their respective objects, as previously described, from non-existent things and from other objects. // 186 //

Having thus refuted falsity, he begins to reject the non-dual reality (sadadvaita) favored by the opponent while establishing the reality of the manifold of difference (bhedaprapañca), starting with the words "sarvāṇyeva" ("all indeed").
Regarding the phrase "yathoditam," it might alternatively be read as "yathāyatham.

The meaning of "yathoditam" is that perception and other means of knowledge do not convey an indefinable (anirvacanīya) object, but rather function without overstepping the limits previously established. // 186 //
For instance, when the cognition "the jar exists here" arises, it does not at that time admit either the non-existence of that jar or its being a cloth. (187)

Regarding what was stated—that it is well known that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) convey a form that is excluded from other entities because their respective objects of cognition do not exist [in those others]—that very point is now established by the words "For instance, here... and so forth.
At present, the cognition "the jar exists here" at that time apprehends the very existence of the jar there by way of its own unique form.

The meaning is that [the cognitions] do not [establish] non-existence (*abhāva*), nor non-being (*asattā*), nor the possession of properties belonging to other entities such as "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*).
Thus, cognitions— such as "the jar exists"— establish the very reality of the object, like a jar, as excluded from the non-existent and excluded from other existing things.
The meaning is that since [statements] such as "the cloth exists" establish only the diversity of existents, non-dual existence (sadadvaita) is not established. // 187 //
As for what was said— that "it exists"— is that [existence] merely the pot itself,
or is it something other than it?
If it were merely that, it would follow that reality is non-dual.
If it is established as a different entity, then it is proven to be distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. // 188 //

Here he raises an objection: "But surely [it exists]. If even by words such as "jar" or "cloth" the word "exists" expresses mere Being (*sanmātra*), then the non-duality of Being (*saddvaita*) is established. If, however, it denotes something distinct from that Being, then it follows that the jar and so forth must be both existent and non-existent, or inexpressible; for by the force of perception, there is an exclusion of their non-existence—this is the sense. (188)
If Brahman exists in this way, then according to the Upanishadic doctrine, Brahman would fall into being indefinable—neither existent nor non-existent—just like a pot. (189)
He refutes this with the words "If it were so.

The meaning is that even Brahman, which is the subject to be established by the Upaniṣads in the statement "Brahman exists," would follow as being indefinable as either existent or non-existent, because it would be subject to the same logic [as the world]. // 189 //
By you yourself, it has been established in this way that even Brahman lacks such qualities, precisely through the Vedic descriptions of bliss, truth, knowledge, and so forth. (190)

Thus, in every such statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇavākya*), there follows the undesirable consequence of a contradictory form; this is what [the author] states with the word "ānanda" (bliss).
In passages such as "Bliss is Brahman," if only bliss and so forth were denoted by the word "Brahman," then the mention of other words would be redundant.
However, if they convey something distinct from that, then it follows that Brahman possesses qualities such as being different from both bliss and non-bliss; this is the meaning.
The meaning is that by the term "bliss" (ānanda), non-bliss is excluded, and by the term "Brahman," bliss is excluded.
The state of not being thus—namely, the absence of bliss and so forth. // 190 //
Furthermore, the statement that the phenomenal world is distinct from both existence and non-existence would be abandoned;
for whatever is asserted in any manner, all things would become exactly like that. (191)
Furthermore, he incurs another undesirable consequence for the opponent by stating "existent or non-existent":
the claim that "the phenomenal world (prapañca) is distinct from both existent and non-existent" would itself fall away from its own intended meaning.

The point is that, according to the method of explanation [already given], what would be established for the phenomenal world is merely its being distinct from that which is distinct from both existent and non-existent.

"Whatever" (yaditi): whatever object whatsoever is expressed in whatever manner—let it follow that all of that is devoid of that very manner in the way you have demonstrated; this is the meaning. // 191 //
Therefore, the cognition "it exists" arising with respect to jars and other objects brings about the realization of the ultimate reality of the specific configuration of each respective entity. (192)

In statements such as "the pot exists," existence-in-itself (*sattāmātra*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), and the difference between the pot and so forth is superimposed (*āropita*); refuting, as it were, what is accepted by others, the author sets forth his own intended meaning with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is clear. // 192 //

The existence of entities, which is established by their respective fixed forms based on the exclusion of similar and dissimilar things—that is "Being" (sattā), and it is not something independent or other [than those forms]. In that case, how can there be any talk of non-duality? (193)
(Thus, by refuting the existence of a real non-duality, the ultimate reality of the manifold of difference is established:
"In its own kind," etc.

The persistence of each respective entity—whether as a relation to time or a relation to a means of valid cognition—is by way of its own unique form, which distinguishes it from both heterogeneous and other homogeneous things.
That is the existence (sattā) of each respective entity; and it is established for every individual object,
being the meaning of a verbal root and dependent upon an agent.
The sense is that, given its existence, independence and non-duality as you intend them are simply not tenable. // 193 //
Nor can the perception of various distinct forms be denied; for it has already been stated previously that what is cognized cannot be a property of the cognition itself.
Has something been established by you regarding consciousness, or not?
If it exists, there would be partiality; if it does not, your labor is fruitless. (195)

Having thus established the plurality of objects of cognition (*prameya*), he now establishes the plurality of cognitions (*pramiti*) by means of the phrase "and not," in order to refute the non-duality of consciousness (*cidadvaita*) favored by opponents.

The meaning is that the plurality of consciousness, which is experienced through the distinctions of its objects and substrates, as well as through its own internal distinctions such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, cannot be dismissed.
Here, having restated the inference stated by opponents regarding the featurelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*) of consciousness, he refutes it with the words "it is not [to be] known" (*na vedya*).
Is the property to be proven—the state of being devoid of distinctions—accepted with respect to consciousness, or not?

If it is accepted, then you fall into the error of partiality toward one property without justification: namely, that one property is established while other properties, even though they are supported by valid means of knowledge, are not established. This is the meaning.

And thus, there would be the consequence of contradicting the admitted lack of distinction; this is the underlying intention (*hārda*). There is an alternative reading: "there would be a sublation of the thesis" (*pakṣabādhaḥ syāt*). If the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is not accepted [as existing], [then the thesis is undermined].
The meaning is that, in that case, the exertion for the sake of proving that [position] would result in futility. // 194 // 195 //

Therefore, cognitions whose internal distinctions are clearly perceived by their own inherent nature do not attain identity with external objects such as jars, any more than they do with external things like chariots [which remain as they are]. (196)
Regarding the word "ataḥ":
the previously printed reading, "yathā rathādibhir vāhyair naikyam yāti," is incorrect.
Therefore—"ataḥ" means because [the opponent's position] has been rejected by such inferences as the fact that consciousness is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*).

Cognitions, which possess their own specificities based on the objects and the substratum and are clearly perceived as distinct, cannot be one with external objects such as jars existing as they are; this introduction is intended to refute the view that there is no difference between the cognition and the cognizer, nor between the act of cognizing and the object cognized. (196)
The rule of simultaneous apprehension certainly does not apply to each individual cognition; for if it did not exist, nothing could serve as the object of cognition, including universals. (197)
Regarding the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*):

the second half of this verse—whether it be "there exists no universal consciousness (*citisāmānya*) which is the locus of all cognition," or "there exists no consciousness accompanied by a universal which is the locus of all cognition"—is not tenable.
It is not logical [to claim] that because the object of knowledge and the knower are apprehended only together with cognition (*saṃvid*), they are non-different.
Because there is no rule of simultaneous apprehension with respect to each specific cognition,
since an object is perceived even by another cognition in the absence of a particular one.

If it is argued that although there is deviation regarding simultaneous apprehension with respect to specific [cognitions], there is nonetheless a rule of simultaneous apprehension with respect to consciousness in its general form (*citsāmānya*), [we reply:]
That too is not correct;
the meaning is that there is no such thing as a persistent universal consciousness (*citsāmānya*) distinct from particularities that could serve as the object of the cognition of all objects.

However, according to the reading as it stands in the manuscript, the meaning is this: if the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) were not established, then the entire collection of knowable things—consisting of both universals and particulars, and comprising both the knower and the known—would indeed exist as something distinct from cognition.
In this way, the validity of the distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*), the knower (*mātṛ*), and the object of knowledge (*meya*) is established.

This verse—from "because of the rule of simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*) up to "the elaboration clearly follows" (*prapañcaḥ sphuṭam añcati*)—is well-integrated with the portion that refutes the opposing view being restated.
Therefore, it should be joined immediately after the final verse concerning the establishment of the consciousness that is being perceived.

And it should be understood that this verse demonstrates the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason consisting in the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), which serves as the proof for the identity of the object of knowledge and the knower through their cognition. // 197 //
Because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, there can be no object other than consciousness;
for that which is independent of anything else in its own manifestation is precisely what the elders declare by the term "self-luminosity. (198)
When one thing does not appear even while another is appearing, the former is not a distinct entity from the latter, just as a false moon is not distinct from the real moon. (199)
If consciousness were not manifesting, there would be no manifestation of the self or its objects;
thus, the phenomenal world clearly approaches the nature of a transformation of pure awareness. (200)
Here, the restatement of the view to be refuted is provided by the phrase "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*), and so forth.

In order to establish that consciousness does not necessarily appear [as an object] when an object is manifested, he states its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) with the words "that which is this" (*yadetad*).

That whose verbal designation is based on the ground for the application of the term "self-luminosity" is "that which has the word 'self-luminosity' as its designation," meaning it is denotable by the term "self-luminous."
By this, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is established.
Regarding the phrase "in which":

since there is no manifestation of the object even in the absence of the manifestation of consciousness, it is proven that the object—whose manifestation is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the absence of the manifestation of consciousness—is non-different from consciousness.
The meaning is that, like a reflection which does not appear within the interior of a mirror, it is non-different from the original object (*bimba*).
Regarding the term "not appearing":
*ātman* is the knower, and *artha* is the object of knowledge.

The world-phenomenon (*prapañca*)— that is, the phenomenal expansion of the known and the knower— is the manifestation (*vivarta*) of consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is the object of superimposition (*āropa*) upon the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that is non-consciousness (*asaṃvid*).
It "extends" (*añjati*), meaning it spreads out or reaches forth.

What is intended here is that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is non-different from consciousness, characterized by its being devoid of any existence apart from the existence of its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

It should be understood that the position of the Yogācāras—that external forms such as blue and yellow are imagined through latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within cognition—and the position of the Māyāvādins—that objects such as blue and yellow are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) therein—are both sought to be refuted here. (Verses 198–200)
Those whose distinctions are being guarded do not follow inference. // 201 //
He refutes this position with the words "Do not [say] so," and so forth. The meaning is: do not disregard—that is, do not reject—the objects characterized as the knower and the known.
Why is their rejection not tenable? To this he replies: "By perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*).

The meaning is that these distinctions between the knower and the known, being protected by the more powerful means of valid cognition that is perception, do not conform to your inference of the identity of consciousness.
And the superiority of perception lies in its being that upon which [other means of knowledge] depend.
For, in order to establish the unity of consciousness regarding objects, one must first apprehend the essential natures of both the objects and the consciousness;
and from that very apprehension, their mutual difference is also established. Thus, the meaning is that inference, being sublated by perception, does not proceed.

The manner in which the dissimilarity between this case and the inference from the distinction of flames is explained is set forth in the *Ātmasiddhi*; it should be investigated from that very source. // 201 //
For in this way, "I know this"—this triad is clearly manifested as distinct from one another; thus, it is directly perceived by everyone through their own self-witnessing. (202)
To explain: "by way of mutual non-identity" means by way of being distinct from one another;
"the triad" refers to the three categories characterized as the knower, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing.

In this regard, the venerable Śrī Paraśarabhaṭṭārya’s wise saying should be reflected upon: "If the distinction between the cognizer ('I') and the cognition ('I know this') were to manifest, then even external objects would have to be one;
if the doctrine of the falsity of the object of knowledge were true, then even valid cognition would be false—if they could endure that, then the lifespan of our doctrine would be long indeed. (202)
Furthermore, inference does not operate when there is direct perception as a counter-argument;
for instance, the non-hotness of fire is not inferred from its being a substance. (203)
Regarding the term *pratyakṣa*:

it means "contradictory" (*pratipakṣa*). What has been stated is that your inference—that there is a unity of consciousness between the knower and the known—is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhita*), just like the inference that fire is not hot. // 203 //
Furthermore, this reason is contradictory, because coexistence belongs to two things;
for even according to you, consciousness does not manifest together with itself. (204)

He says "furthermore" (kiñca) to state that some literary evidence, which establishes a distinction between cognition and its object by functioning as a reason for their difference, is contradictory to the proof of their non-difference.
For even you do not accept that "cognition is perceived together with cognition";
rather, the point is that the collection of objects being perceived simultaneously with that cognition must necessarily be distinct from it.
A continuous stream of pure consciousness, free from the disturbances of blue and other [objects], shines forth during sleep and similar states;
however, an object does not appear thus as something separate from cognition.
Therefore, consciousness is real, but the object of consciousness is unreal. // 205 //
Here he raises an objection: "In the case of the appearance of blue and so forth... [The opponent argues: "Cognition appears even in states such as sleep without the coloring of an object;
however, an object never appears without cognition."
The meaning is that the collection of objects, being superimposed upon consciousness, is false, just like its reflection. // 205 //
This is merely the prattle of one who has not reflected upon the contradiction of his own words;
for if this were so, the rule of the necessary co-perception [of subject and object] would be lost.
"He avoids this [objection]" means:

if consciousness were to appear without an object, then the appearance of the object without that [consciousness] would also be almost established; thus, the reason you stated—namely, "the inseparable simultaneous perception"—is unproven.
By speaking in this way, you yourself have not even considered the contradiction between your own preceding and subsequent statements. This is the sense. // 206 //
That which appears without [the existence of] something else, yet also appears even without that [other thing],
is like a jar appearing by itself even without a cloth or other objects. (207)
(Thus ends the demonstration of the reality of the distinction between cognition, the cognizer, and the cognized, by means of the refutation of the non-duality of consciousness.
"This much alone is perceived as the portion of consciousness that possesses the nature of an established entity.

Thus concludes the *Saṃvitsiddhi* within the *Siddhitraya*, which was composed under the guidance of the venerable Paramācārya Śrīmad Bhagavat Yāmunamuni, the preeminent leader in propagating the illustrious doctrine of Viśiṣṭādvaita.
He establishes the very non-establishment of the reason with the words "yasmāt" (since).
The word "nirbhāta" is in the ablative case derived from a present participle; thus, it means "from that which appears."

Just as the manifestation of a cloth is established apart from a jar, and the manifestation of a jar is established apart from that [cloth], so too the manifestation of an object is established apart from knowledge, because it manifests without [the mediation of] knowledge; thus, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is not established for the blue object and its cognition.

Now, since the illumination of an object must be expressed as being by means of knowledge alone, and since knowledge is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), the manifestation of the object cannot exist without the manifestation of knowledge.

If it is argued that this is not tenable, even so, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is indeed untenable, whether with respect to a particular cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*) or a general cognition (*jñānasāmānya*).
In the former case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); in the latter case, it is unestablished (*asiddha*) according to the opponent's own view.
This is the point of verse 197: "The rule of simultaneous apprehension refers only to this object."
And it has already been stated that this [point] must be investigated here.

Thus, it should be understood that the established conclusion is that the true nature of the distinction between the means of knowledge, the knower, and the object of knowledge cannot be denied. // 207 //

This one of great fame, Rāmānujārya, the preeminent teacher and treasury of wisdom— who descended into the noble lineage of the author of the Śrībhāṣya and is expert in clarifying the true meaning of the Śrībhāṣya— is now shining brightly in the city of Bhūtapurī.
Having attained awakening through service at the lotus-feet of that [teacher], and having taken refuge in the venerable father known as Kṛṣṇārya,
I— whose name is celebrated as Aṇṇaṅgarārya— have, by the grace of the feet of my Guru, composed this commentary which serves as a boat upon the ocean of Yāmuna’s words;
this beautiful exposition has been fashioned for the satisfaction of the Guru’s feet.
But whatever virtues are found herein, they are born of the grace of the Teacher; however, the faults are my own—thus should it be reflected upon by those possessed of discernment.
This necklace of flowers, consisting of words, is offered upon the chest of Śrī;
may Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, be pleased by this.
This work was completed in the Vikrama year [indicated by] the seasons, the sky, the pits, and the eyes (2006),
on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, in the city of Vṛttālaya.

Thus, by the illustrious Śrī Kṛṣṇamācārya, the preeminent teacher and ornament of the lineage of Prativādibhayankarācārya, born in the divine land of Śrī Nagapurī (Tirunāṅgūra), and a master of the four systems of philosophy...

The venerable Āsūri Rāmānujācāryadeśika, who descended from the divine lineage of the illustrious Bhāṣyakāra—the embodiment of compassion whose fame rests upon the horizons reaching to the farthest ends of the earth; who was a delighter in residing at the sacred city of Bhūtapurī; and who was a universal scholar among the learned and a descendant of Hārīta.

By the venerable Vaiṣṇava servant, Pra. Bha. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya, whose heart was [familiar] with the Nyāya, Vyākaraṇa, and the systems of logic (*pramāṇatantra*) acquired through the joy of serving the lotus feet of his preceptor—
The *Siddhāñjana*, a commentary on the *Saṃvitsiddhi* composed by Śiromaṇi, the scholar of both Vedāntas,
is hereby completed.
May he be victorious! May he be most victorious!
